Where we are going

What a claim-evidence map is — and where it comes from
Why it belongs in comparative politics specifically
The anatomy of one

You will build one of these for every numbered session. They are ungraded — and they feed the quizzes, the cold calls, your presentations and your paper.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1 — Where it comes from

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
An honest opening

“Claim-evidence map” is not a term with its own scholarly literature. It is a teaching device, assembled from two established sources.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Source 1 — Toulmin’s layout of arguments
Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (Cambridge University Press, 1958; updated edition 2003).
Toulmin’s insight: arguments have functional parts, and most disagreements are really disagreements about one particular part.

Claim — what you are asserting
Data — what you are asserting it on
Warrant — why the data bears on the claim
Backing — why the warrant itself holds
Modal qualifier — how strongly you assert it
Rebuttal — the conditions under which it would not hold



A note on terms: Toulmin wrote data in 1958. “Grounds” came later, in Toulmin, Rieke and Janik, An Introduction to Reasoning (1979). If you cite the 1958 book for “grounds,” you will be citing it for something it does not say.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Source 2 — the Claim–Evidence–Reasoning framework
McNeill, Krajcik and Hershberger, Supporting Grade 5–8 Students in Constructing Explanations in Science: The Claim, Evidence, and Reasoning Framework for Talk and Writing (Pearson, 2011).
Three parts:

Claim — a statement answering the question
Evidence — data supporting the claim
Reasoning — “a justification that shows why the data count as evidence to support the claim” (McNeill et al. 2006, p. 158)



That third element is Toulmin’s warrant under another name. CER is a deliberate simplification — it drops the qualifier and the rebuttal.


Our version puts them back. In comparative politics you cannot afford to drop the rebuttal.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Does mapping actually work?
The claim that mapping improves reasoning is itself an empirical claim — so it should be treated like one.

van Gelder (2005) argues gains come from deliberate practice, not exposure. Making the structure visible is what makes practice possible
Twardy (2004) reports gains of roughly 0.7–0.85 standard deviations across the Reason! studies, against about 0.3 SD for typical critical-thinking instruction and about 0.34 SD for a full first year of undergraduate education



For argument mapping in political science teaching specifically, see Rousseau and van Gelder (2025), Journal of Political Science Education 21(3): 406–422.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2 — Why comparative politics?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Lijphart’s problem, again
Recall the central methodological problem of the field: too many explanatory variables, too few cases (Lijphart 1971).


The statistical method
Controls for rival explanations by design — many cases absorb the work.

The comparative method
Two cases. Control comes from case selection, and everything else falls on the quality of each inferential link.



With a large N, a weak link is diluted. With two cases, a weak link is the argument.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: So the map is not a study aid
text:
So the map is not a study aid
In a regression, the reader can inspect your specification. In a two-case comparison, the reader can only inspect your reasoning — if you have made it inspectable.

It forces you to state the claim as one contestable sentence
It forces every number to carry its year, source and caveat
It forces you to name the warrant — the step students skip most often
It forces you to write down the counter-evidence before you are attached to your answer



King, Keohane and Verba (1994) argue that qualitative and quantitative work answer to the same standards of inference. The map is how a two-case study meets them.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The part everyone skips

The warrant. Students give a claim and three facts and believe they have argued something. They have not — they have put a claim and some facts on the same page.


The warrant answers: why does this fact bear on that claim?


No warrant
“Ghana has alternated four times. Kenya twice. Ghana has a presidential run-off.”

Warrant supplied
“A run-off forces a losing plurality candidate to face a second contest he can win, which lowers the cost of accepting defeat the first time.”



The second version can be attacked. That is what makes it an argument.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Not all evidence does the same work
text:
Not all evidence does the same work

Van Evera (1997, pp. 31–32) named the four tests; Bennett (2010, p. 210) recast them as a 2×2 on whether passing is necessary and/or sufficient for the inference; Collier (2011, p. 825) adapted that table. The necessary/sufficient framing is Bennett’s, not Van Evera’s.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Why the tests matter to you
text:
Why the tests matter to you

An evidence row that does not say what kind of work it does is a row that has not been thought about.


Most of what you find early is straw-in-the-wind. Say so — it is honest, not weak
A hoop test is the most useful thing you can build: it lets you eliminate a rival explanation, and elimination is the scarcest good in a two-case design
A smoking gun is worth ten straws — but its absence proves almost nothing
If you think you have a doubly decisive test, you have probably misread the evidence

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4 — How to build one

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Six moves









Move
Test of whether you did it




1
Write the question the reading or the session poses
It ends in a question mark and is about why, not what


2
Write a claim — one sentence, contestable
Someone reasonable could disagree with it


3
List evidence, one row each: value · year · source · caveat
You opened every source yourself


4
Write the warrant under each row
It says why this bears on that, not what the fact is


5
Write the counter-evidence and the rival explanation
You can name what would make you abandon the claim


6
Add a qualifier
The claim is no longer stated more strongly than the evidence allows





Twenty to forty minutes. It is not an essay. If it is taking two hours, you are writing prose instead of mapping.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The standing rule

Never write down a number you have not opened the source for. Every figure carries three things: the year, the source, and the caveat.


Your dossier is built to make this concrete: it reports figures that disagree with each other, and it ends with a page headed “What we could not verify.”



A quotation that is not on the page you cite is a provable problem — whatever produced it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5 — A worked example

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The question and the claim
Question. Why has Ghana alternated power four times since 1992 while Kenya has alternated twice?


Claim. Ghana’s presidential run-off lowers the cost of accepting defeat, which explains its more frequent peaceful alternations — while Kenya’s single-round threshold with a county-distribution rule raises the stakes of the first count.



One sentence. Contestable. Names a mechanism, not a correlation.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The evidence rows









Evidence
Year · source
Caveat
Test




Ghana: 4 alternations (2000, 2008, 2016, 2024); Kenya: 2 (2002, 2022)
1992–2024 · electoral commissions
The outcome being explained, not evidence for the mechanism
—


Ghana has held 2 presidential run-offs (2000, 2008); Kenya has held 0
Dossier Kenya_Ghana
Both Ghanaian run-offs coincide with alternations — suggestive, and small n
Straw


Kenya’s threshold: 50%+1 and 25% in 24 of 47 counties
Const. 2010, Art. 138(4)

Hoop (fails)





Row 3 is the useful one. If Kenya had no distribution rule, the claim would be eliminated. It clears the hoop — which does not make it true.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The counter-evidence

Sequence. Ghana’s peaceful alternations began in 2000 — before most of the institutional differences took their current form. Kenya’s devolution began in 2013 — after the violence it was designed to prevent.



The opinion data cut the wrong way. Ghana scores far better on every expert measure — Freedom House 80/100 against Kenya’s 49/100 in 2026. Yet on Afrobarometer Round 10, Ghanaians report lower satisfaction with democracy (49.2% v. 51%) and lower trust in the electoral commission (28.5% v. 36%).


Ghana’s fieldwork closed before the December 2024 election and the alternation that followed — so the comparison is not clean. Say that out loud rather than hiding it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The rival explanation


The institutional story
The run-off does the work.

The demographic rival
Ghana: Akan 45.7%; top three groups 78.1%. Kenya: largest group 17.1%; top three 44.7%.
One group near half the population makes two-party competition possible. Kenya’s fragmentation makes coalitions necessary — ENPP ≈ 4.0 against Ghana’s 1.83.



Both ENPP figures are the instructor’s own Laakso–Taagepera calculations from published seat counts, not published values. If you use them, present them as calculations.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The qualifier — and what it costs
text:
The qualifier — and what it costs

Qualified claim. In the Kenyan and Ghanaian cases since 1992, run-off provisions appear to be associated with lower-cost alternation — but the association is confounded by ethnic demography, and the sequence of Ghana’s alternations precedes the institutional differences invoked to explain them.


That is a weaker sentence than the one we started with. It is also the only one the evidence will carry.



Learning to write that sentence — and to be unembarrassed by it — is most of what this course is teaching.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The four failures








Failure
What it looks like
The fix




The topic, not the claim
“Devolution in Kenya”
A sentence someone could disagree with


Facts without warrants
Three true statements, no link
Under each row: why does this bear on that?


Naked numbers
“Gini 38.5”
38.5, 2022, World Bank — Ghana’s is 2016, six years apart


No counter-evidence
Every row supports the claim
If you cannot say what would change your mind, you have a preference, not an argument





The fourth is the one that separates good teams from fluent ones.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What to carry forward

The map is Toulmin’s layout, simplified by CER, with the rebuttal put back
It matters here because the comparative method has too few cases to dilute a weak link
The warrant is the part you will skip; write it anyway
Evidence is not uniform — ask what work each row does: straw, hoop, smoking gun
Every number carries year, source, caveat
Write the counter-evidence before you fall in love with the claim

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Who participates, and who is represented — and does the way a society is organized explain democracy independently of its history, economics and culture?


Chapter 5 was held back until now on purpose. The background chapters gave you history, economics and culture. This one adds social structure, and it bears directly on the question of representation that the institutional chapters have been circling.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 5, pp. 118–133.
Ishiyama’s definition is plain: social structure is “the way in which society is organized.” Societies may be hierarchical, as in caste systems, with layers of groups one above another; or more egalitarian, with little distinction in superordinate or subordinate status.
Three issues only, and he says so: feudalism, inequality, and civil society. Keep the deck to that spine and students will keep the chapter.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class you should be able to:

Explain what cross-cutting cleavages are and why pluralists think they help democracy
State the case that feudalism helped democracy and the case that it hurt it — and Moore’s way of resolving them
Give Dahl’s two mechanisms linking extreme inequality to dictatorship
Define civil society, and say what it excludes
Distinguish Almond’s four types of interest group
Explain social capital and Putnam’s four causes of civic decline
Separate Civil Society I, II and III, and state the endogeneity problem that hangs over all three

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: Social structure and pluralism

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The chapter’s spine






Figure 1: Social structure, and the three issues Chapter 5 limits itself to. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 118–119.
Put this up before anything else and leave it up. Ishiyama says plainly that although many approaches connect social structure to regime type, “in this chapter we limit ourselves to three issues” — feudalism, inequality, civil society. Students who can name the three can navigate the chapter; students who cannot will read it as a list of names.
The bottom row of each column is the argument’s current state, not its origin. Worth pointing at when you reach each part.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The claim

The structure of societies shapes the kinds of political systems that emerge — independent of political culture and economics.



Marx: conflict between groups, especially classes, is the prime determinant of the political system that emerges — though those conflicts were primarily economic
Huntington (1984): democracy is facilitated by a widely differentiated and articulated social structure with relatively autonomous social classes, regional groups, occupational groups, and ethnic and religious groups




The pluralist version: what best promotes democracy is a large number of relatively autonomous associational groups — independent of the state, and a way for citizens to articulate interests. Trade unions, gun clubs, professional associations, athletic groupings (Almond 1958).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Why pluralism is supposed to work
text:
Why pluralism is supposed to work







Cross-cutting cleavages
People of different races, ethnicities or classes find themselves sharing recreational interests or bound together in a union. Those ties cut across social, ethnic, racial and religious differences, promoting tolerance and acceptance


Limiting state power
Autonomous groups let society control the state — and democratic institutions are the most effective means of exercising that control





And the contrapositive, which is the claim that actually does the work: societies without such autonomous groups are far more likely to be dominated by a centralized state, or an authoritarian or totalitarian dictatorship.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 118–119; Almond (1958); Huntington (1984).
Cross-cutting is the concept to drill, and it is the direct counterpart of Chapter 4’s polarization. Cleavages that reinforce one another — same people on the same side of every divide — produce two blocs. Cleavages that cross-cut leave everybody sharing some group with everybody else. Same demography, opposite politics.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: what makes a cleavage cross-cutting?
text:
Note: what makes a cleavage cross-cutting?
A cross-cutting cleavage is one where:

The cleavage is politically irrelevant and therefore harmless
Every major social division separates the same people into the same two camps
The groups involved are too small to affect national politics
Membership in one group cuts across membership in another, so people who differ on one divide share another



Shared membership across divides. The second option describes reinforcing cleavages — which is Chapter 4’s polarization arriving under a different name.


[Key] Option 4. Option 2 is the exact inverse and the most instructive wrong answer, because a student who picks it has the right concept and the wrong sign.
Make the link explicit: Collier and Hoeffler’s two-bloc danger from Chapter 4 is a society whose cleavages reinforce. Pluralism’s bet is that enough associational life will scramble them.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Feudalism

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Feudalism cuts both ways







Feudalism helped
An early form of pluralism that limited the development of centralized state power — so such systems were likelier to evolve into democracies than those lacking that social pluralism. The record of Western Europe against Russia, and Japan against China, suggests something to it (Moore, from Chapter 2)


Feudalism hurt
Tocqueville: the absence of feudalism helped democracy in the United States, because there were no embedded hierarchies preventing social and political mobility. The persistence of feudalism in Latin America is held up as the counter-example





The resolution: the question is not whether feudalism existed but what kind existed. For Moore (1966), English democracy turned on the transformation — the commercialization — of the English feudal lords, who became the basis of the bourgeoisie. Not so elsewhere, and certainly not in Latin America.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 119–120; Moore (1966); Tocqueville.
This is Chapter 2’s England-and-France comparison returning with the social structure made explicit, so it should feel familiar. The wool-and-enclosures chain from the Chapter 2 lecture is the mechanism underneath this slide.
The teaching value is the shape of the move: two flatly contradictory findings, resolved not by picking a winner but by discovering that the variable was mis-specified. That is a pattern worth naming — it is the same move Przeworski and Limongi make on modernization theory.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
“No bourgeois, no democracy”

Moore’s own restatement of the proposition, in its more limited formulation.


So the key to democracy is a large indigenous bourgeoisie — which ties the economic system, the social structure and the political system into one chain.


Why a market economy supplies the social base (Lipset 1961):

A market economy requires a dispersion of economic power and some form of private property — and dispersed economic power creates alternative centres of political power that check the state
Market economies are likelier to produce sustained growth than command economies — and wealth creates the desire for wealth protection, which gives rise to social organizations


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 120–121; Lipset (1961).
Note the parenthesis Ishiyama includes and students skip: centrally planned economies are often able to promote rapid growth over short periods. The claim is about sustained growth, not growth.
The second mechanism is the subtler one and the one that connects to Part 4 — property to protect is a reason to organize, and organizations are what civil society is made of.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: what does Moore’s formula mean?
text:
Note: what does Moore’s formula mean?
Moore’s “No bourgeois, no democracy” claims that democracy requires:

A large indigenous commercial middle class, which in England grew out of the commercialization of the feudal lords
An urban industrial working class organized into parties
The absence of a feudal past
A market economy, regardless of which classes it produces



A large indigenous bourgeoisie. The English lords became that class; elsewhere — Latin America above all — feudal elites stayed feudal, and no such class appeared.


[Key] Option 1. Option 3 is Tocqueville’s claim, which the chapter presents as the rival; a student who takes it has read half the argument.
The word indigenous earns its place. A commercial class that is foreign, or that depends on the state, does not do the work — which is where this connects to Chapter 3’s comprador bourgeoisie.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: Inequality

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Inequality and democracy
Since Aristotle, the argument has run in both directions: by reducing inequalities in the distribution of political power, democracy helps reduce inequalities of wealth and status (see also Mill 1862).

Running the other way: extreme inequalities in wealth undermine democratic political structures. Aristotle pointed to the importance of a large middle class — a sentiment echoed much later by Lipset (1959).



Dahl (1971, ch. 6) gives two mechanisms by which extreme inequality produces dictatorship.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Dahl’s two mechanisms







From above
Concentrated economic resources make the “haves” unwilling to accept reform or extend rights to the “have nots,” believing the have nots will deprive them of their wealth. Concentrated wealth in a few hands undermines meaningful democracy


From below
Inequality produces high resentment among the “have nots” — likely to translate into violence, or at minimum to undermine the legitimacy democracies depend on





And the asymmetry that makes it a regime question: an authoritarian government can repress reactions against inequality; a democracy cannot indefinitely repress and remain democratic.




“The effect of inequality on democracy is anticipated because concentrated economic rewards lead to similarly concentrated political resources, undermining political equality. And economic inequality generates frustrations that undermine allegiance to democratic procedures.”
Bollen and Jackman 1985, p. 440

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: Dahl’s asymmetry
Why, on Dahl’s account, does extreme inequality threaten democracies more than it threatens dictatorships?

Dictatorships usually have less inequality to begin with
A dictatorship can repress the reaction to inequality; a democracy cannot repress indefinitely and remain a democracy
Inequality is harder to measure in democracies, so the effect is overstated
Democracies redistribute, which provokes the wealthy into mounting coups



The repression asymmetry. Both regime types face the resentment; only one can suppress it without ceasing to be itself.


[Key] Option 2. This is the item that separates students who followed the argument from those who remember “inequality is bad for democracy.”
Press on the implication for their reform packages: a proposal that raises inequality is not regime-neutral. It loads a pressure a democracy has fewer legitimate tools to contain.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: Civil society

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What is civil society?

LSE Centre for Civil Society: an “arena of uncoerced collective action around shared interests, purposes and values. In theory, its institutional forms are distinct from those of the state, family and market, though in practice, the boundaries … are often complex, blurred and negotiated.”



Diamond (1994): “the realm of organised social life that is voluntary, self generating, self supporting, autonomous from the state, and bound by the legal order or set of shared rules … citizens acting collectively in a public sphere to express their interests, passions, and ideas … make demands on the state, and hold state officials accountable. It is an intermediary entity, standing between the private sphere and the state.”


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 121–122; Diamond (1994).
Diamond’s last clause is the one to underline — an intermediary entity. Civil society is defined by its position between two things, which is why the next slide, on what it excludes, is not pedantry.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What civil society is not
Civil society focuses on expressly public and political goods, not private ones. So the concept excludes:

Family life
Inward-looking group activity
The profit-making enterprise of individual firms — organizations that pursue private gain



It is also distinct from political society — groups directly tied to the state: Congress, the bureaucracy, political parties. Civil society shapes political society, but is conceptually distinct from it.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, p. 122.
Three categories, and students routinely collapse them: society at large (everything), civil society (voluntary, public-facing, outside the state), political society (inside or attached to the state). A church bake sale, a tenants’ union, and a congressional caucus are one of each.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: which of these is civil society?
text:
Note: which of these is civil society?
On the chapter’s definition, which belongs to civil society?

An independent tenants’ association lobbying the city on housing policy
A political party contesting national elections
A family-run firm pursuing profit
A congressional caucus organized around a shared policy interest



The tenants’ association. Voluntary, autonomous from the state, pursuing a public good — while the caucus and the party are political society, and the firm pursues private gain.


[Key] Option 1. Every distractor fails on a different criterion, which is the point of the item: option 4 is inside the state, option 3 is private gain, option 2 seeks office rather than influence.
That last distinction is the chapter’s own: civil society groups “do not seek to win formal office but rather seek to influence those in office.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three spheres






Figure 2: What the concept of civil society includes, and the two things on either side of it that it excludes. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, p. 122; Diamond (1994).
The whole definitional section is on one slide here. The left column is what the chapter excludes because it pursues private gain or looks inward — family life, inward-looking group activity, and the profit-making enterprise of individual firms. The right column is political society, excluded because it is part of the state or seeks to become it.
Ask the class to place three cases out loud: a church bake sale, a tenants’ union, a congressional caucus. One of each.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
An old idea
The concept long predates the 1990s revival.







Socrates
Truth is discovered through open public argument via the dialectic; public argument ensures civility in the body politic


Plato
A just society is one where people work for the common good and practice civic virtues — wisdom, moderation, justice


Aristotle (c. 335 BC)
Citizens must know each other’s character and preferences to choose leaders well; the polis is an “association of associations” enabling citizens to share in ruling and being ruled


Cicero
Societas civilis — a good society ensuring peace and order among the population





But the classical notion did not distinguish society from the state. That separation waits for the Treaty of Westphalia in 1648 and the sovereign state it recognized.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Hobbes and Locke: society gives life to the state
text:
Hobbes and Locke: society gives life to the state
Westphalia let monarchs build central control — national armies, professional bureaucracies, absolutism outside England. Enlightenment thinkers responded.







Hobbes
A champion of absolutism seeking a rational basis for it. In the state of nature life is “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short”; reason persuades people to surrender sovereignty to a common power. A civil society existed prior to and apart from the state, and its formation produced government, state and laws — which then sustained civility


Locke
Writing to justify replacing James II in 1688. The state of nature is unpleasant but not inevitably a state of war; people would leave it only for a better way to protect life, liberty and property — which an absolute monarch is not. Two treatises: people submit to a common authority, and that authority is limited and may not threaten basic rights





Both arrive at the same structural claim from opposite politics: society gives life to the state, and the state is charged with protecting civil society.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Tocqueville and Durkheim
Alexis de Tocqueville (1840) wrote at length on the necessity of civil associations for democracy.

Americans joined voluntary organizations of all kinds, from social clubs to service organizations
That rich associational life led to the blossoming of democracy in the new republic
Associations let citizens overcome their lack of influence as separate individuals; as associations grew, the state and other actors were forced to notice and recognize their preferences


Durkheim ([1893] 1984): connections between individuals remain after the initial interaction. Those lasting ties shape the social capital that results, so associations persistently affect one another through the impact individuals make on each other.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Almond’s four interest groups
Twentieth-century political scientists identified civil society as made up of interest groups. Almond (1958) distinguishes four.

Built from Ishiyama ch. 5, after Almond (1958)








Type
Organization
Basis
Example




Anomic
Almost none — dissipates once the fury of the mob is spent
Spontaneous collective response to a frustration
Organized protest, riots


Non-associational
Generally unorganized; activity depends on the issue at hand
Common kinship or identity ties — race, ethnicity
—


Institutional
Mostly formal
Has some other political or social function besides the interest
Caucus groups in Congress; bureaucratic agencies


Associational
Highly organized — internal hierarchy, steady funds
Formed explicitly to represent a set of issues
Free trade unions, gun or animal rights groups, professional organizations





Associational groups are the ones that matter for democracy, and the feature that separates them from institutional groups is independence from the state — they influence its actions without being part of it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: institutional or associational?
What distinguishes an associational interest group from an institutional one?

Associational groups are bound together by kinship or ethnic identity
Associational groups are larger and better funded
Associational groups are formed spontaneously in response to a grievance
Associational groups are independent of the state, rather than being part of it



Independence from the state. Both types are highly organized and well funded — which is exactly why the second option fails, and why the real line is structural, not a matter of size.


[Key] Option 4. Option 3 describes anomic groups and option 1 non-associational ones, so the item sweeps the whole typology.
The chapter is careful on the point students over-read: independence does not mean these groups have no effect on the state. It means they are not part of it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Civil society as a school for democracy
text:
Civil society as a school for democracy
Almond and Verba (1963) — the same pair as Chapter 4 — argued voluntary associations were the most important mediating factor between individuals and the state.







Resources
Associating gives a person political resources usable toward their own goals


Attitudes
Membership shapes political attitudes; the political element of many organizations produces better awareness, better voting choices, more participation, more accountability


A check on authority
Associational groups monitor the state continually, subjecting leaders to popular scrutiny


Dense networks
Multiple channels to voice opinions and articulate interests give individuals a reason to engage


A school for democracy
Working together in the Boy Scouts, a union or a professional body teaches cooperation, teamwork and compromise — and supplies the main channels for leadership training and political recruitment

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Putnam: social capital
Robert Putnam (1993, 1995): even non-political organizations are vital — bowling leagues, sporting clubs — because they build social capital, trust and shared values that transfer into the political sphere.








Physical capital
Machines, economic inputs — raises productivity


Human capital
An educated workforce — raises productivity


Social capital
How a society is organized — also raises productivity






What made the American economy and state strong was dense social networks producing norms of social trust that facilitated coordination and cooperation for mutual benefit — an echo of Tocqueville a century and a half later.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 126–128; Putnam (1993, 1995); Coleman (1988); Uslaner (2002).
The Italian study is the comparative payoff and worth a minute: self-help organizations and community policing in the north produced both a stronger democratic impulse and an economic and industrial powerhouse, against an impoverished and historically state-dominated south. One country, two social structures, two outcomes — a controlled comparison inside a single state.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Why civil society declined
Putnam’s metaphor is the decline of organized bowling leagues: Americans join far less than in Tocqueville’s time, and are becoming less trusting and more disengaged.

Movement of women into the labour force. Women had comprised the bulk of voluntary organization membership; their entry into the workforce reduced women’s civic participation and family participation overall
Greater mobility. Post-war transport ended the pattern of being born, living and dying in one neighbourhood — and with it the social bonds of identifiable communities
Other demographic changes. Fewer marriages, more divorces, and movement from urban neighbourhoods to impersonal suburbia
Technological transformation and the privatization of leisure. Television, video games, DVDs, the internet — one can be completely alone to be entertained



The implication: decline in civic engagement, and ultimately in the health of democracy in the developed world.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What the decline looks like






Figure 3: Putnam’s four causes of civic decline, and what they add up to. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 128–129; Putnam (1995).
Four drivers, none of them political — women entering the labour force, post-war mobility, demographic change and suburbia, and the privatization of leisure. That is the detail worth pressing: Putnam explains a political decline entirely by non-political causes, which is the same move that makes his main argument work and the same move the critics attack.
Ask which of the four students think has done the most work since 1995. The fourth has arguably changed beyond recognition.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: Putnam’s bowling leagues
Putnam uses bowling leagues as evidence for a claim about democracy because:

Bowling league membership correlates with turnout across American states
Leagues were among the few associations open to women before the 1970s
Even non-political associations build social capital — trust and shared values — that transfers into the political sphere
Bowling leagues were historically a recruiting ground for party activists



Even non-political groups build social capital. That is the move that makes the argument interesting and the one that makes it vulnerable — the critics’ question is whether the transfer happens at all.


[Key] Option 3. Option 4 inverts the claim into a conventional political-recruitment story, which is precisely what Putnam does not need to assume.
Flag the vulnerability now, because the critique slide pays it off: Foley and Edwards ask whether participation in a bowling league is necessarily and inevitably connected to political participation. If the transfer fails, the whole argument fails.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: The critique

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Are dense networks a good thing?
text:
Are dense networks a good thing?







Schattschneider (1960)
Interest groups are elite groups, motivated primarily by private interest rather than the public good


Olson (1965)
By the logic of collective action, small well-organized groups dominate the political process, leaving many voices unheard


Lowi (1969)
“Interest group liberalism” — groups pursuing progressive goals produce status quo conservatism, since they protect what they have once they achieve it





So interest group pluralism came under fire as undemocratic: the special interests it represents detract from democracy.




Nor is there any reason in principle why dense networks should make a democratic state more efficient. The “counterweight of civil society” may be a burden — dense webs of association that leach off resources and threaten the smooth and equitable function of the modern state.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three civil societies
Foley and Edwards (1996) find two conceptions in the literature — potentially contradictory. Booth and Richard (1998) add a third.

Built from Ishiyama ch. 5, after Foley and Edwards (1996) and Booth and Richard (1998)








Emphasis
Relation to the state




Civil Society I
Associational life fosters patterns of civility; a socializing and educating force promoting tolerance and cooperation
Positive effects of association with governance


Civil Society II
Civil society as a counterweight to the state — independent by definition, promoting accountability and checking tyranny
Separate from the state


Civil Society III
Voluntary associations that are revolutionary in nature, and do not promote democracy
Dense civic networks may turn separatist, centrifugal and divisive in weak or unstable systems — especially deeply ethnically divided ones





I and II contradict: one needs civil society close to the state to socialize good citizens, the other needs it apart from the state to check tyranny. It cannot be defined as both at once.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 129–131; Foley and Edwards (1996); Booth and Richard (1998).
Civil Society III is the corrective to a literature that had quietly assumed all association is benign. Dense networks in a deeply divided society can organize the division rather than dissolve it — which is Chapter 4’s polarization reappearing as a civil society problem.
And note the condition Ishiyama attaches: for civil society to work at all there must be political peace and some degree of openness.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The contradiction, drawn






Figure 4: Civil Society I, II and III — and why the first two cannot both be right. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 129–131; Foley and Edwards (1996); Booth and Richard (1998).
The arrows carry the argument. Civil Society I points toward the state — association works by socializing citizens into civility, which requires proximity to governance. Civil Society II points away — it works by checking tyranny, which requires independence. Both are in the literature, often in the same paragraph, and they prescribe opposite things.
Civil Society III sits underneath because it is not a third position in that argument; it is a reminder that association can organize a division rather than dissolve it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The endogeneity problem

“The strength and responsiveness of a democracy may depend on the character of civil society, as Putnam argues, reinforcing both the democratic functioning and strength of the state. But such effects depend on the prior achievement of both democracy and a strong state.”
Foley and Edwards 1996, p. 281



Which caused which? Did civil society cause democracy in the West, as Tocqueville and Putnam suggest — or did a democratizing state give rise to civil society?




This is more than academic. Unless the relationship is understood, it is difficult to contend civil society causes anything at all — which calls into question every civil-society-building programme run by organizations such as USAID.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 131–132.
Name it as reverse causation and point back to Chapter 4: this is Barry’s objection to the civic culture, in a new setting, with a policy budget attached. Same logical structure, same remedy — find variation that lets you separate the two.
That last sentence is the one that makes the methodological point land for undergraduates. An unresolved causal direction is not an abstraction when hundreds of millions of aid dollars rest on one reading of it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Which way does the arrow run?
text:
Which way does the arrow run?






Figure 5: The endogeneity problem, and the policy that rests on it. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 5, pp. 131–132; Foley and Edwards (1996, p. 281).
Name it as reverse causation and point back to Chapter 4 — this is Barry’s objection to the civic culture in a new setting.
The orange band is what makes it land for undergraduates. An unsettled causal direction is not an abstraction when hundreds of millions of aid dollars rest on one reading of it. Ask what evidence would settle it, and let them discover that the answer is over-time variation of exactly the kind a two-case design cannot supply.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two more criticisms







Overstated attachment
Stolle and Hooghe (2003): the impact of social capital outside the group setting is weak, if it exists at all. They urge a focus on the internal workings of groups rather than pronouncements about civil society as a whole. Foley and Edwards (1996): focusing on non-political organizations underestimates participation in explicitly political ones — and there is no necessary connection between civic engagement and political engagement


Measurement
How do you measure social capital? Surveys make cross-country comparison hard, since ideas do not transfer. Counting groups raises questions of which groups to include, how to distinguish types, and whether to include a time element. Social networks are hard to measure because the connections are intrinsically weak





Not insurmountable — but they must be considered in evaluating what researchers conclude.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: the strongest objection to Putnam
text:
Note: the strongest objection to Putnam
Which objection most directly threatens the core of Putnam’s argument?

Social capital is difficult to measure across countries
There is no necessary connection between civic engagement and political engagement
Dense networks can become separatist in divided societies
Interest groups are elite-dominated and serve private interests



The missing link. Putnam’s whole claim is that non-political association transfers into political life. If the transfer does not happen, the bowling leagues explain nothing — the others weaken the argument; this one removes its mechanism.


[Key] Option 2. Every option is a real criticism from the chapter, which is what makes this a reasoning item rather than a recall one — students must rank objections by what each would destroy.
Option 4 attacks the value of civil society, option 1 attacks our ability to test it, option 3 limits its scope. Only option 2 severs the causal chain Putnam needs.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Where this leaves the argument

Ishiyama’s summing up: little consensus on the effects of civil society on the development of democracy — but considerable agreement it has some effect.


What he does commit to:

Where political cultures value tolerance, moderation, compromise and civility, democracy is easier to develop — and civil society helps promote those values
Whether civil society promotes democracy or democracy promotes civil society is not always clear
But there is consensus that civil society helps maintain democracy




Note the retreat in that last line. The strong claim was that civil society builds democracy; the claim that survives is that it sustains one.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s article: Clayton and Zetterberg
“Quota Shocks” — gender quotas as a shock to who gets represented, and what follows.

A quota changes descriptive representation by design and by a known date — which is what makes it usable as an identification strategy rather than just a policy
The question is what happens downstream: whether changing who sits in the legislature changes what the state spends on and does



Read it against this chapter. Ishiyama’s social structure arrives through voluntary association — slow, self-generating, hard to engineer. A quota is the opposite: representation altered by institutional fiat, and therefore testable.


Two reasons it belongs here.
First, substance: the chapter asks who gets organized and who gets heard, and answers in terms of associational life. Quotas supply a different lever on the same outcome, and let students see that “who is represented” has both a societal and an institutional answer.
Second, method: a quota adopted at a known moment is close to a natural experiment, and students should by now be able to say what that buys — the same move as Posner in Session 5. Ask what is held constant and what varies.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Does economic development cause political development — and if it does, in which direction does the causal arrow run?


Ishiyama surveys three answers that disagree about almost everything: where to look, what the unit of analysis is, and whether the Western path can be repeated at all.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 3.
Frame it against Chapter 2. There, the explanation was historical sequence. Here, the explanation is economic structure — and the three schools fight over whether that structure is internal, international, or something the state itself can choose.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class you should be able to:

State what modernization theory claims and name the main versions of “political development” inside it
Distinguish social mobilization from political institutionalization, and explain why Huntington needs both
Explain how dependency theory inverts the modernization story
Say what statism adds that neither of the other two can explain
Compare all three on the dimensions in Table 3.4
Separate endogenous from exogenous democratization, and say which one Przeworski and Limongi’s evidence supports
Define state making as Tilly uses it, and explain why he calls European state institutions byproducts
Place a bureaucracy on Fukuyama’s two dimensions, capacity and autonomy

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: Modernization theory

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Older than political science
Modernization theory is “less a coherent theory than an approach.” Its roots run back to the Enlightenment conviction that people can change their own conditions.







Condorcet
Technology and economic transformation let humankind alter its moral and cultural values


Saint-Simon (1760–1825)
Economic development and technology can better social conditions


Comte (1798–1857)
Modernization ushers in a “positive” scientific era


Marx
Industrialization of the economic base changes the social and political superstructure





The common thread: economic change comes first, and political change follows.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Durkheim: complexity and anomie
Durkheim asked what industrialization does to the division of labour.

All societies must perform certain functions — security, political leadership, spiritual leadership
What differs is the complexity of the division of labour that performs them
Simple societies need little complexity to hold order; industrial capitalism forces functional differentiation



Anomie. Older certainties — God above all — are called into question by science and technology, producing a widespread sense of rootlessness, and with it criminality and social violence.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3; Durkheim ([1893] 1964).
Connect back: this is the same disruption Chapter 2 called the storm. Durkheim gives it a psychological mechanism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Parsons: traditional and modern as ideal types
text:
Parsons: traditional and modern as ideal types
Table 3.1 · Traditional vs. modern societies









Traditional societies
Modern societies




How is social status determined?
Ascriptive status
Achievement status


What social roles do people play?
Diffuse roles
Specific roles


Are values universal or case-dependent?
Particularistic values
Universalistic values


Which matters more, group or individual?
Collectivity orientation
Self-orientation


Immediate reward, or postponed for future benefit?
Affectivity
Affective neutrality





These are ideal types anchoring a continuum, not descriptions. No society is purely one or the other — every real society sits somewhere between.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Table 3.1, after Parsons (1951, 1971).
Ishiyama is careful here and students often are not: ascription has not vanished from modern societies — he names race, ethnicity and gender explicitly — and achievement is not absent from poor ones.
Affectivity vs affective neutrality is the row worth explaining: in traditional societies people act to meet immediate needs; in modern ones, basic needs being met, people forgo present satisfaction for future gain. Mill called it enlightened rationality.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Lipset: the strong claim
In Political Man (1959) Lipset argued for a direct relationship between industrialization and political democracy.

Economic modernization creates the social requisites of democracy: a large, vibrant, literate middle class, and wealth
He found direct correlations between democracy and higher urbanization, higher literacy, and greater per capita income



From correlation he concluded causation: economic development has a direct causal relationship with political democracy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Deutsch: not democracy — mobilization
Karl Deutsch (1961) accepted the disruption but refused Lipset’s conclusion.

the process in which the major cluster of old social, economic and psychological commitments are eroded or broken and people become available for new patterns of socialization and behavior
— Deutsch (1961, p. 494), defining social mobilization


Industrialization moved populations from countryside to city. People who had identified with a locality now made new acquaintances, learned new things, and questioned their own identity — which is how national identities emerged.



Politically, mobilization expands “the politically relevant strata of the population” — those persons who must be taken into account. Whether that ends in stability or disorder depends on how the existing system copes.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Almond and Coleman: five crises
Economic modernization creates crises a political system must resolve. What results depends on how it copes.







Crisis
What it is




Identity
Local ties break; a new sense of community — usually national — must form


Legitimacy
Divine right gives way to the idea that rule rests on the consent of the governed


Participation
A “revolution in rising expectations” generates demands to take part in governing


Penetration
New institutions must link rulers to ruled directly, replacing indirect rule through nobles


Distribution
New social groups demand their material share of the economic pie




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, citing Almond and Coleman (1960; text gives 1966), The Politics of the Developing Areas.
The penetration crisis is the one students find least intuitive. Before modernization, kings ruled through local nobles who collected the taxes and kept considerable autonomy — including warring with each other. Direct rule had to be built.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What is “political development”?
The term does not mean one thing, and the disagreement matters.


Lipset
A politically developed state is one that is democratic.

Beer (1973)
Development is the expansion of the bureaucratic state — patterns of interests create patterns of power, which generate new interests, ad infinitum.

Huntington (1965, 1968)
Development is political institutionalization: “the process by which organizations and procedures acquire value and stability.”



Notice what follows. On Beer’s and Huntington’s definitions, a country can develop politically without becoming any more democratic.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Huntington’s four dimensions
How do you tell whether a political system is institutionalized?







Dimension
The question




Adaptability / rigidity
Can it survive a change in its environment?


Complexity / simplicity
Is there a division of labour, with redundant structures?


Autonomy / subordination
Is it independent of any single social group?


Coherence / disunity
Is there a unity of purpose holding it together?




Adaptability has three measures: chronological age, generational age (how many leadership transitions), and functional age (how many times it has changed what it does).

Ishiyama’s example for functional age is worth telling. The YMCA began as a religious body for young Christian men, took on recreation, then women, then everyone — and survives as something quite different. The Women’s Christian Temperance Union achieved national prohibition in 1919, could not adapt to another function, and disappeared.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: what does institutionalization measure?
Huntington’s generational age measures a system’s adaptability by counting:

The number of years since the organization was founded
The number of leadership transitions it has been through
The number of times it has changed its function
The number of social groups it represents



The second. A system can be chronologically ancient and still fragile if one leader has never been replaced.


[Key] The second. The first is chronological age and the third is functional age — both are real Huntington measures, which makes them good distractors; the student has to keep three similar terms apart.
Ask for a contemporary example of an old system with a low generational age. It is a fast route into the succession problem, which their China/Vietnam and Hungary/Poland teams will meet directly.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two variables, four outcomes
Table 3.2 · Huntington’s classification of regime types




Institutionalization high
Institutionalization low




Social mobilization high
Civic
Corrupt (praetorian)


Social mobilization low
Contained
Primitive




Table 3.3 · Country examples









Institutionalization high
Institutionalization low




Social mobilization high
The United States · Great Britain · the Soviet Union
Most of the developing world


Social mobilization low
Contained — perhaps colonial societies
Traditional agrarian monarchies (Imperial Ethiopia)






Outcomes are the product of the interaction of the two, not of either alone. Mobilization without institutions is not development but decay.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The entry that should stop you
text:
The entry that should stop you

The Soviet Union is filed under civic — beside the United States and Great Britain.


Ishiyama’s reasoning: the USSR modernized massively and fast in the 1930s, generating extensive mobilization pressure. The system was complex, autonomous, and armed with a legitimising ideology, so it met those demands — or contained them by repression and violence — and survived.



Britain and the United States built institutions before industrialization, which Chapter 2 treated as something close to a historical accident. The Soviet Union built the state and transformed the economy at the same time — rather like building a ship in a stormy sea.


This is the payoff slide for the whole first half. It also shows the cost of Huntington’s definition: if development is institutionalization rather than democracy, a totalitarian state can be a developmental success.
Worth naming aloud: Huntington, at least in the 1960s work, appeared to favour a one-party solution for the developing world. Ishiyama lays out the argument — one-party states are more complex than personalist dictatorships, allow interests to be articulated internally, are autonomous, and rely on rules rather than individuals — and notes India’s Congress, Japan’s LDP, and Mexico’s PRI as long dominant-party cases.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Modernization theory in summary
Whatever version, three commitments recur:

Political development is a consequence of economic development — the political system evolves in response to economic stimuli
The approaches rest on historical observation of the West, particularly Europe
The key intervening variable is often political culture — the subject of Chapter 4



Point 2 is the opening dependency theory will attack, and it is the same parochialism Macridis complained about in Chapter 1.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Dependency

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: A different room, a different answer
text:
A different room, a different answer
While modernization theory developed among North American political scientists, a rival grew in post-war Latin America, rooted in neo-Marxism and dissatisfied with the international economic order.







Prebisch (1950)
Research at ECLA: falling wealth in poor countries correlates with rising wealth in rich ones


Baran (1957) · Frank (1966, 1967)
International capitalism produced the de-development of the developing world


dos Santos (1970)
A “new dependency” — external relations are articulated internally


Cardoso
Growing disparities between centre and periphery, written in exile


Wallerstein (2004)
The “World System” and the history of international capitalism




Cardoso is worth a sentence: he wrote as a dependency theorist in exile and later served as President of Brazil — and governed as something closer to an orthodox reformer. Students enjoy the irony, and it opens the question of whether the theory implies any workable policy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The development of underdevelopment
Frank’s claim, introduced to an American audience in 1966: poverty in the developing world is not a starting condition that development will cure. It is a product of world capitalism.


The Indian textile case. Before the British East India Company, textile production — largely household industry — employed a great many people and was extensive. Cheap manufactured imports followed the British, destroyed the indigenous industry, and created mass unemployment and poverty.



So the periphery is not “behind.” It was actively de-developed.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Two more breaks with modernization theory
text:
Two more breaks with modernization theory
1 · The international system is missing. Modernization theory explains development by internal structural factors, with no reference to the international environment.

2 · The Western path is assumed repeatable. Marx himself wrote, in the 1867 preface to Das Kapital, that “the country that is more developed industrially only shows, to the less developed, the image of its own future.”



Dependency’s reply: the West industrialized before the world capitalist system consolidated — indeed the West created it. Countries developing now face an obstacle their predecessors never had to pass.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Figure 3.1 · Imperialism, nineteenth century






Figure 1: Recreated from Ishiyama, Figure 3.1. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Figure 3.1 and surrounding text.
Note for the instructor: the source file we worked from carries the chapter’s text and tables but not its artwork, so this diagram is a faithful reconstruction from the caption and the paragraphs around it, not a scan of the original.
The line to land is the last one. The surplus does not merely enrich the core — it is spent on reform at home, which is why the revolution Marx predicted in the industrial core did not arrive.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Figure 3.2 · Neo-imperialism, twentieth century






Figure 2: Recreated from Ishiyama, Figure 3.2. FDI, foreign direct investment. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Figure 3.2 and surrounding text. Reconstruction, as above.
The maquiladora example does the work: parts are farmed out rather than finished goods produced, so the value added — and the profit — is captured on the other side of the border. Ask what a country could do about that, and you have arrived at statism before the next section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Figure 3.3 · The internal articulation






Figure 3: Recreated from Ishiyama, Figure 3.3. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Figure 3.3; Amin (1974, 1976); Frank (1967). Reconstruction, as above.
This is the figure that explains why dependency theory is a theory of politics and not only of economics. The comprador bourgeoisie is the hinge: a propertied class with no interest in dismantling the order that enriches it, allied with feudal landlords, and hostile to empowering the masses.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Why dependency implies authoritarianism
In the West the bourgeoisie was the progressive class — it dismantled feudalism and opened the way to democracy.

In the periphery the comprador bourgeoisie is nothing of the kind. Its wealth comes from trade, not industrial production, so it has no reason to change the system, and every reason to keep the masses unempowered.



And if a populist leader does emerge from the masses — usually through the ranks of the military — he is likely to reject bourgeois democracy as Western and corrupt. So from this perspective there is little hope for democracy while dependent relations persist.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: what does “de-development” claim?

Poor countries have not yet begun the development process
Poverty in the periphery is a product of the expansion of world capitalism, not a starting condition
Development stalls because peripheral states adopt the wrong values
Peripheral countries will eventually resemble the core, as classical Marxists expected



The second. The periphery is not behind. It was actively made poor.


[Key] The second. The third is modernization theory’s answer, and the fourth is the classical Marxist expectation — Lenin, Luxemburg, Kautsky — which neo-Marxist dependency theory explicitly denies.
That fourth option is worth dwelling on: classical Marxists expected capital to relocate to the periphery as wages rose in the core, eventually producing a peripheral bourgeoisie and proletariat and the conditions for international revolution. Dependency theory says that never happens.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: Statism

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The anomaly
Classical dependency says the periphery can never catch up. But some countries plainly did.

Japan · Russia · Turkey, and more recently the Asian Tigers — Taiwan, Singapore, South Korea.


Scholars trained in the dependency tradition — Evans, Rueschemeyer, Skocpol — began to question whether dependency travelled beyond Latin America. Some peripheral countries were catching up, and doing it through state-led industrialization.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What both other theories missed
The statist critique: modernization theory and dependency theory are both society-centred. Each ignores the role the state itself plays in capital accumulation and investment.



Liberal state
An arena in which interests compete.

Marxist state
A tool of the dominant class.

Weberian state
“A human community which claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.”




In the first two the state is an object with no interests of its own. For Weber it is a community — so it has interests, and the paramount one is survival.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Politics as the cause
What drives a state to modernize is the threat posed by external enemies. Rapid industrialization raises military capacity, and military capacity buys security.


So the arrow reverses. For modernization theory politics reflects internal economic change; for dependency it reflects external economic structure. For statism, politics is a cause of economic transformation.


Link forward to the team project. Statism is the school that gives a constitutional engineer something to do — it is the one that treats state action as a choice rather than a reflection. That is the same move the course makes in Chapter 1’s neo-institutionalism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: Comparing the three

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Table 3.4 · The three approaches compared










Modernization theory
Dependency
Statism




Unit of analysis
State
Global system
State


Can earlier models be replicated?
Yes
No
Yes


Economic development is possible…
when modern values are adopted
only when the international economic order changes
as the result of voluntaristic action by the state





Read the middle row as the fault line. If earlier models cannot be replicated, then every reform proposal built on a Western template is answering the wrong question.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Table 3.4.
For modernization theory the models are the developed West; for the statists they are the state-led industrializers — Japan, Turkey. Same answer on the row, different exemplars.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: whose unit of analysis?
Which approach takes the global system rather than the state as its unit of analysis?

Modernization theory
Dependency theory
Statism
All three, since each studies countries in an international context



Dependency. For modernization theory and statism alike the unit is the state — development is a function of what happens inside a country’s borders, or of what its state chooses to do.


[Key] Dependency theory. The fourth option is the plausible-sounding trap: it is true that all three are aware of the international environment, but only dependency theory makes the world system the thing being analysed.
This is the item most worth connecting to their own projects. A team whose diagnosis is entirely domestic has implicitly chosen modernization theory or statism — and should say so rather than stumble into it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: Testing the claim

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
One correlation, two explanations
Lipset’s finding — richer countries are more often democratic — is not in dispute. Przeworski and Limongi (1997) point out that it is also not self-explaining.








Endogenous democratization
Development causes democratization. As a dictatorship grows richer, it becomes more likely to become a democracy. This is modernization theory


Exogenous democratization
Democracies arise for all sorts of reasons, more or less independently of development — but once established, they are far more likely to survive where incomes are high






Both stories predict the same correlation. That is precisely why the correlation cannot settle the question.


[Sources] - Przeworski and Limongi, “Modernization: Theories and Facts,” World Politics 49 (1997). - Ishiyama ch. 3, on Lipset.
This is today’s article, and it is the sharpest test anyone has run on the material in Part 1 of this lecture. Set it up as a problem of under-determination: the observation is agreed, the explanations are incompatible, and the observation is consistent with both. That structure recurs everywhere in this course.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What the data say
Przeworski and Limongi’s answer, from regime histories across the developing and developed world since 1950:

Transitions to democracy are not reliably more likely as dictatorships grow richer
But democracies die at low incomes and almost never die at high ones



No democracy in the sample ever fell in a country richer than Argentina in 1975 — a per capita income of $6,055.



So the correlation between wealth and democracy is produced mainly by where democracies survive, not by where they are born.

[Sources] Przeworski and Limongi (1997); the $6,055 figure recurs in Przeworski et al. (2000) and is reported in Haggard and Kaufman, which your students met on Quiz 2.
Worth connecting explicitly: Haggard and Kaufman’s point that the consensus is far stronger for consolidation than for transitions is this finding, restated.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: which explanation survives the test?
text:
Note: which explanation survives the test?
Przeworski and Limongi’s evidence supports:

The endogenous explanation — as dictatorships grow richer they democratize
Both explanations about equally
Neither; the association disappears once region is controlled for
The exogenous explanation — development does not make democracy more likely to arrive, but makes it far more likely to last



The exogenous explanation. Development does not reliably produce transitions; it protects democracies that already exist.


[Key] The exogenous explanation. The first option is the classic modernization claim — the one most students will carry into the reading from the first half of this lecture, which is exactly why it is here.
Press the class on what this does to modernization theory. It does not refute it so much as relocate it: economic development still matters enormously to democracy, just not at the moment modernization theory said it did.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: what would the rival predict?
text:
Note: what would the rival predict?
If the endogenous explanation were correct, what should we observe?

Rich countries are democratic more often than poor countries
The rate at which authoritarian regimes transition to democracy rises as their income rises
Democracies in rich countries last longer than democracies in poor countries
Democracies grow economically faster than dictatorships



Rising transition rates with rising income. The first option is the thing to be explained, not a test — and the third is what the exogenous story predicts.


[Key] Option 2. This is the harder of the two items, because it asks for reasoning from a theory to its observable implication rather than recall of a conclusion.
The method lesson is the transferable one, and it is worth stating in one sentence: when two explanations imply the same correlation, ask what else each implies, and go look there. That is the move Round 3 asks of every team.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 6: Before development, the state

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A prior question
All three approaches in this lecture assume something they do not examine: that there is a state — one that can tax, enforce, and act on whatever strategy it adopts.


Statism makes the state the explanation of development. Tilly and Fukuyama ask where the state itself came from, and what makes one capable.



These were the readings for Session 3 · September 24, and they sit on this quiz block. Ishiyama has no chapter on state capacity, which is why the two articles carry it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Tilly: four activities
Charles Tilly (1985), “War Making and State Making as Organized Crime.” European rulers did four things:







War making
Eliminating or neutralizing rivals outside the territory they claimed


State making
Eliminating or neutralizing rivals inside that territory


Protection
Eliminating or neutralizing the enemies of their clients


Extraction
Acquiring the means of carrying out the first three





Note what state making means here. It is not building a bureaucracy — it is winning the internal fight. The bureaucracy comes later, and comes by accident.


[Sources] Tilly, “War Making and State Making as Organized Crime,” in Evans, Rueschemeyer and Skocpol, eds., Bringing the State Back In (1985), pp. 169–191.
Students reliably assign the administrative meaning to “state making,” and the error is worth correcting on the spot, because the whole argument depends on the distinction. Adjudication, distribution and production arrive later, as the state acquires functions it never set out to have.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: what does “state making” mean?
In Tilly’s usage, state making refers to:

Constructing the bureaucratic and fiscal machinery through which a ruler governs
Securing the consent of the governed through representative institutions
Eliminating or neutralizing rivals inside the territory the ruler claims
Eliminating or neutralizing rivals outside that territory



Rivals inside the territory. The fourth option is war making; the first is what state making produced rather than what it denotes; the second is the social-contract story Tilly is writing against.


[Key] Option 3. The first option is the intuitive answer and the one most will choose. Take a minute on it: if state making meant building administration, Tilly’s argument would be circular — states built states.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The racket, and the byproduct

“Someone who produces both the danger and, at a price, the shield against it is a racketeer.”


Banditry, piracy, gangland rivalry, policing and war making, Tilly argues, belong on the same continuum — and war making and state making are “quintessential protection rackets with the advantage of legitimacy.”



The consequence that matters. Rulers did not set out to build states; they set out to make war, which required extraction, which required bargaining with the populations they extracted from. Taxation systems, courts, assemblies — and eventually rights — emerged from that bargaining as unintended byproducts.


[Sources] Tilly (1985), pp. 169–172, 181–186.
Two things worth adding.
First, on legitimacy, Tilly follows Stinchcombe: what matters is less the consent of the governed than the assent of other authorities — the probability that other authorities will confirm a given authority’s decisions. That is a deflationary account of legitimacy and it is useful against students who treat legitimacy as a feeling.
Second, the bargaining mechanism is the reason the essay is assigned rather than merely cited. Rights were not granted; they were the price of money.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Why Europe’s bargain may not repeat
text:
Why Europe’s bargain may not repeat
Tilly’s warning about the contemporary developing world:

European rulers had to extract the means of war from their own populations, and had to concede to get them
Today’s state builders can obtain military power from outside — arms, training, subsidy, alliance



Where coercive capacity arrives from abroad, the bargain is never struck — and the historical link between making war and extending citizen rights is broken.


This is the slide to connect to the dossiers. Any team whose focal country has an externally supplied security apparatus — and that is most of the post-colonial world — is looking directly at this mechanism.
It is also a warning about the method of this whole lecture. Europe’s sequence is not a template; it is one path, run under conditions that no longer obtain.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Fukuyama: what is governance?

Governance is “a government’s ability to make and enforce rules, and to deliver services” — regardless of whether that government is democratic or not.



It is a property of the executive and its bureaucracy, not of the regime
A government can be democratic and badly governed, or authoritarian and well governed
It is about the performance of agents in carrying out the wishes of principals, not about the goals the principals set




So the common practice of folding “voice and accountability” into a governance index makes it impossible to ask whether democracy improves governance — the answer has been built into the instrument.


[Sources] Fukuyama, “What Is Governance?” Governance 26, no. 3 (2013).
The target is the Worldwide Governance Indicators and their relatives. The complaint is conceptual before it is empirical: a measure that includes the independent variable cannot test the hypothesis.
Fukuyama surveys four ways of measuring governance quality — procedural (Weberian criteria such as meritocratic recruitment), capacity (resources and professionalization, including tax extraction), output (results actually delivered), and autonomy. He is sceptical of pure output measures, since outputs are jointly produced by the state and the society it acts on.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Capacity and autonomy
Fukuyama’s proposal: locate any bureaucracy on two dimensions.







Capacity
Resources and professionalization — can it actually do things?


Autonomy
How much discretion it has, versus how tightly rules and political principals bind it





There is no single right amount of autonomy. The optimum is conditional on capacity: give a low-capacity bureaucracy wide discretion and you get predation; bind a high-capacity one in detailed rules and you waste the expertise you are paying for.


[Sources] Fukuyama (2013).
His example of the second failure is legislative micromanagement of capable American agencies; his example of the first is any weak state given a free hand. The relationship is an inverted U — for each level of capacity there is an optimum, and the optimum rises with capacity.
The payoff for this course: “weak institutions” is not a diagnosis. Capacity and autonomy are separable and separately observable, and a state can be low on one and high on the other.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: how much autonomy is right?
text:
Note: how much autonomy is right?
On Fukuyama’s account, the optimal degree of bureaucratic autonomy:

Is as high as possible, since autonomy insulates officials from political interference
Depends on capacity — less discretion for low-capacity bureaucracies, more for high-capacity ones
Is as low as possible, since unelected officials should be tightly bound by rules
Is set by regime type, with democracies requiring less autonomy than autocracies



It depends on capacity. Fukuyama refuses both unconditional positions — and the first and third between them are what most readers bring to the article.


[Key] Option 2. Options 1 and 3 are the two standing positions in the public-administration literature, and the item tests whether students noticed that the article declines both.
