For the dossiers: ask each team whether their focal country’s problem is capacity, autonomy, or the mismatch between them. That is a sharper Round 2 sentence than anything with “weak institutions” in it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Where this leaves the argument

Ishiyama’s own summing up: there is broad consensus that the economic environment is a crucial explanatory factor for the emergence of political forms, including democracy — while the debate over how it matters remains open.


But the test tightens the claim. Przeworski and Limongi’s evidence says development does not reliably produce democracy — it protects it. And Tilly and Fukuyama put a prior condition under all three approaches: none of them works without a state capable of acting.


Chapter 4 turns to the variable modernization theory kept treating as the intervening step: political culture.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
For your dossier
Round 2 asks for a context diagnosis including political economy. This chapter gives you three incompatible ways to write that section.
Three things to try this week:

Ask which of the three approaches your focal country’s trajectory best fits — and which one your comparator fits. If they differ, that difference is your Round 3 argument
Locate your focal country on Huntington’s two dimensions. Is its problem mobilization, institutionalization, or the gap between them?
If your team is drawn to a structural explanation, name the mechanism linking structure to politics. Haggard and Kaufman’s complaint about structural theories was precisely that the mechanism goes missing
Say whether your focal country’s state capacity problem is capacity, autonomy, or the mismatch between them. “Weak institutions” is not a diagnosis
If its security apparatus is externally supplied, Tilly predicts something specific about the bargain that was never struck. Check whether the record bears it out

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
For next session
Session 5 · October 8 — When do identities become political?

Ishiyama, Chapter 4: Political Culture and Ethnopolitics
Due: claim-evidence map
Quiz 3 at the start of the meeting
Group B · Round 2 presentations



Chapter 4 takes up the intervening variable this chapter kept deferring — and asks whether culture explains anything that economics has not already explained.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Lecture 1: What does comparison explain?

Comparative politics is both a subject and a method.


By the end of today, you should be able to:

distinguish comparative politics from country description;
explain the many variables, few cases problem;
recognize most-similar and most-different designs; and
connect the field’s history to our constitutional-engineering project.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Open with the central question and preview the four learning outcomes.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Start with a comparison


Taiwan

Semi-presidential system
Mixed electoral rules
Competitive democracy


South Korea

Presidential system
Mixed electoral rules
Competitive democracy




What could this pairing help us explain—and what could it not establish by itself?


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Take two quick responses. The aim is to surface the difference between noticing variation and designing a comparison.
[Sources] - Instructor application of Ishiyama’s comparative-method framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The book begins with a problem
text:
The book begins with a problem
Ishiyama does not organize the course as a tour of countries.

He organizes it around a practical question:

Under what conditions can political democracy develop—and when will institutional engineering fail?




Theories become useful when applied to a consequential problem.
Institutional choices must fit historical, economic, social, cultural, and international conditions.
Democracy is not assumed to be easy, inevitable, or universally transplantable.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Emphasize problem-based learning and the conditional—not prescriptive—character of the question.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction, opening section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A problem-based course
Problem → diagnose a focal country’s political constraints
Comparison → use a shadow case to test explanations
Design → evaluate institutional alternatives and trade-offs
Defense → explain why the recommendation fits the evidence


The goal is not to discover a perfect constitution. It is to make a defensible comparative claim.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Connect the chapter directly to the semester project.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction, opening and “The Plan of this Book.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Defining comparative politics

Transition: We know the course problem. Now define the field that will help us solve it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three definitions compete

The study of foreign countries
The study of comparative government
A subject and method of political inquiry



Ishiyama adopts the third definition: systematic comparison of political phenomena within political systems.



The United States is therefore one case among many—not a separate universe.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Cold call: Which definition would exclude the United States, and why is that limiting?
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Subject and method work together


As a subject
Political phenomena within a state, society, country, or political system:

institutions;
behavior; and
political ideas.


As a method
Systematic comparison used to:

identify similarities and differences;
discover patterns; and
explain variation.



Suggested time: 2 minutes. Stress that a country report is not automatically comparative politics.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), drawing on Wiarda, Mahler, and Lim.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Comparative politics asks “why?”


Description
How does a legislature work?
Who selects the executive?
What electoral formula is used?

Explanation
Why did this institution emerge?
Why does it produce different outcomes elsewhere?
Under what conditions will it change?



Description supplies evidence. Comparison turns evidence into an explanation.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Ask students to turn one descriptive question into an explanatory question.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Macridis and the traditional approach.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Within states—or between them?







Comparative politics
International relations




Politics primarily within political systems
Politics primarily between political systems


Elections, parties, courts, executives, identity, participation
War, alliances, trade, diplomacy, international organizations


Why outcomes vary across cases
Why states and other actors interact as they do




The boundary is useful, but not absolute: international forces also shape domestic politics.

Suggested time: 1.5 minutes. Use EU politics or foreign election interference as a boundary case.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The comparative method

Transition: The field’s subject is broad. Its distinctive leverage comes from research design.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The central constraint
Imagine explaining the Russian Revolution with one case.

Military defeat and wartime strain?
Economic and social transformation?
Bolshevik organization and Lenin’s leadership?
Paralysis at the top of the imperial regime?



Many plausible causes + one observed outcome = weak causal leverage.



Lijphart’s formulation: comparative politics often has too many variables and too few cases.

Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Cold call: Why can evidence consistent with a theory still fail to prove that theory?
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Lijphart (1971).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three strategies for causal leverage








Strategy
How it controls alternatives
Main constraint




Experiment
Randomization and a control group
Countries cannot usually be assigned to treatments


Statistical method
Estimates several relationships at once
Requires enough cases and defensible measures


Comparative method
Selects cases to hold key factors constant
Conclusions depend heavily on case-selection logic





The comparative method is a quasi-experimental strategy for a small number of cases.


Suggested time: 3 minutes. Briefly distinguish experimental control, statistical control, and control by case selection.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of experimental, statistical, and comparative methods.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Most-Similar Systems Design
Compare cases that are similar on relevant background conditions but differ on the outcome or institution of interest.


Similar cases + different outcome → investigate the remaining difference.



This is Mill’s Method of Difference.

Strength: controls many rival explanations through case selection.
Risk: the cases may differ in an unnoticed but consequential way.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Introduce MSSD as a logic, not a claim that cases are identical.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), MSSD discussion.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Estonia and Latvia illustrate MSSD
Both cases shared important conditions before the Soviet collapse:

annexation in 1940;
indigenous and Russophone populations;
relatively high Soviet-era development;
unitary, roughly parliamentary systems.










Key difference
Latvia
Estonia




1989–90 electoral rule
Single-member plurality
Single Transferable Vote





Different party-system development could then be investigated through the electoral-rule difference.

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Stress “investigated,” not mechanically “proved.” Ask what omitted difference might still matter.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Estonia–Latvia example; Ishiyama (1993).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Cold call: defend a pairing
Return to Taiwan and South Korea.

What important conditions does the pairing approximately hold constant?
What institutional or political difference could provide leverage?
What unmeasured difference could undermine the comparison?



A defensible comparison identifies both its leverage and its limits.


Suggested time: 3 minutes. Cold-call one student for each question, then invite one amendment from the room.
[Sources] - Instructor application of Ishiyama’s MSSD framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Most-Different Systems Design
Compare cases that differ widely but share the same outcome.


Different cases + same outcome → search for a common cause.



This is Mill’s Method of Similarity.

Strength: a shared factor may travel across diverse contexts.
Risk: different causal paths can generate the same outcome.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Introduce equifinality: the same outcome can have multiple causes.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), MDSD discussion.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Design check
Scenario A
Two economically and culturally similar democracies adopt different electoral systems and develop different party systems.
Scenario B
Three societies with different histories, economies, and institutions all experience democratic breakdown after elected leaders disable checks and balances.

Which is MSSD? Which is MDSD? What would each comparison need to measure?

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Ask for the design first, then the dependent variable and candidate explanatory factor.
[Sources] - Instructor examples based on Ishiyama’s comparative-design framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
How the field evolved

Transition: The field’s history is a recurring debate over what counts as knowledge and what political inquiry is for.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two tensions organize the history


Normative ↔︎ empirical
Should scholars ask what political order ought to be—or explain what can be observed?

Understanding ↔︎ application
Is the purpose to build general knowledge—or improve political institutions?



Comparative politics repeatedly moves between these poles rather than permanently choosing one side.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Use these tensions as the thread through the historical sequence.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “The Evolution of Comparative Politics.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Plato and Aristotle offer two traditions
text:
Plato and Aristotle offer two traditions


Plato

Knowledge through reason and insight
Emphasis on justice and the ideal order
Foundation of a normative tradition


Aristotle

Approximately 150 constitutions as evidence
Comparison of institutions and social foundations
Foundation of an empirical tradition



Both nevertheless asked how political life might be improved.

Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Use the cave briefly, but do not let it displace the comparative point.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Plato and Aristotle.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Aristotle classified regimes



Rule by
Public-serving form
Self-serving form




One
Monarchy
Tyranny


Few
Aristocracy
Oligarchy


Many
Polity
Democracy




For Aristotle, “democracy” meant corrupt rule by the many—not the modern idea of constitutional democracy.


His larger claim: mixed government supported by a strong middle class was more stable than pure oligarchy or pure democracy.

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Clarify the historical meaning of “democracy” before students interpret the table using modern definitions.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Aristotle and Table 1.2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Comparison revived with a changing world
text:
Comparison revived with a changing world

Exploration exposed Europeans to political systems beyond Europe.
Modern states developed distinct institutions, economies, and political cultures.
Renaissance science restored confidence in observation and systematic inquiry.




Machiavelli
Compared political practices to find models that rulers could emulate.

Montesquieu
Compared political systems and advanced separation of powers—but also made dubious climate-based claims.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Use climate theory as a reminder that comparison can generate bad inference as well as insight.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Middle Ages and Enlightenment discussion.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Marx and Weber disagree about causation
text:
Marx and Weber disagree about causation


Marx
Economic relations and class power shape political and social institutions.
Primary causal emphasis: political economy

Weber
Culture, religion, institutions, and political leadership have partly autonomous effects.
Primary causal emphasis: multicausal explanation


Cold call: What evidence would distinguish these explanations?

Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Ask students to name an observable implication rather than choose a favorite theorist.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Marx and Weber.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The American field started descriptively
Early twentieth-century American comparative politics largely emphasized:

European governments;
formal and legal institutions; and
description of legislatures, executives, and courts.


World War II and the Cold War increased demand for knowledge about:

rebuilding Germany and Japan;
Soviet and communist politics;
decolonization and political instability; and
democratic development.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Note how world events and funding priorities shaped the field’s agenda.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), American comparative politics and the behavioral revolution.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Categories can distort what we observe
text:
Categories can distort what we observe
Ishiyama recounts an example from precolonial West Africa:

some communities selected “kings” by rotation among notable families;
British officials interpreted kingship as hereditary;
indirect rule converted a rotating office into a life appointment inherited by heirs.



Using a familiar European label obscured the institution—and colonial policy then changed it.



Comparison requires concepts that travel without erasing local meaning.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Treat this as the chapter’s warning about conceptual stretching and parochialism.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), West African example in the Macridis discussion; Crowder (1968).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The behavioral revolution changed the unit of analysis

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Easton put politics inside an environment
text:
Easton put politics inside an environment
Environment supplies demands and support
↓
Political system converts inputs into authoritative decisions
↓
Outputs reshape society and the international environment
↺ Feedback creates new demands and support

The system includes government, parties, interest groups, and leaders—not only formal institutions.

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Walk once around the input–conversion–output–feedback cycle using a tax-policy example.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Easton’s systems approach and Figure 1.1.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Easton’s “black box” remains a problem
The systems model clarifies interdependence, but it leaves major questions open:

What actually happens inside the conversion process?
Why do political systems process similar demands differently?
Can the model explain democratic collapse or institutional change?
Does naming a system’s components produce a testable explanation?



A framework organizes observation; a theory must also specify causal expectations.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Distinguish a conceptual framework from a causal theory.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), critiques of Easton’s systems approach.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Structural functionalism looks beneath labels
Almond and Coleman asked two separate questions:

What structures exist?
What political functions must be performed?


The same function can be performed by different structures:

parties may aggregate interests in one system;
the military, a ruling party, or patronage networks may do so elsewhere;
courts, bureaucracies, or party organs may regulate and adjudicate.


Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Emphasize that similar institutional names do not guarantee similar functions.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), structural-functionalism discussion; Almond and Coleman (1960).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Political systems must perform recurring functions
text:
Political systems must perform recurring functions


Process functions

Interest articulation
Interest aggregation
Policy making
Regulation
Adjudication


System-maintenance functions

Political socialization
Recruitment of leaders
Political communication



Cold call: Which structures perform these functions in China? In Taiwan?

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Accept multiple answers; press students to separate the function from the organization performing it.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Almond’s structural-functional framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Structural functionalism also has limits

It assumes system survival is the central goal.
It can portray political systems as static rather than adaptive.
Its categories may reflect Western democratic experience.
It says little about how institutions emerged or changed.



The field escaped narrow formalism, but risked replacing it with abstract concepts that explained too little.


Suggested time: 1.5 minutes. Link the critique back to Macridis: every framework highlights some phenomena and obscures others.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), critique of structural functionalism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Post-behavioralism reopened purpose
Critics challenged two behavioralist commitments:

Value-free science: political facts require interpretation, and interpretation cannot be fully separated from values.
Method over substance: technical refinement can displace consequential political questions.


Post-behavioral and constructivist approaches emphasized how political realities and categories are socially constructed.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Avoid presenting this as a rejection of evidence; it is a dispute over objectivity, meaning, and purpose.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), post-behavioral critique; Bay (1965).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Neo-institutionalism brought rules back in
Behavioralism looked beyond formal rules; neo-institutionalism asked what had been lost.


Electoral systems shape representation and party competition.
Executive design shapes coordination and deadlock.
Federal arrangements distribute authority and conflict.
Courts and constitutions structure enforcement and restraint.




Institutions matter because people can redesign rules more readily than they can redesign history, culture, or economic structure.


Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Stress that institutions interact with context; rules are malleable but never unconstrained.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), neo-institutional movement and constitutional design.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The field comes full circle
Ancient question: What political arrangement supports a good and stable order?
Behavioral correction: Explain politics empirically, beyond formal rules.
Neo-institutional synthesis: Use comparative evidence to understand how rules shape outcomes in context.


Comparative politics becomes applicable again—but with greater methodological discipline.


Suggested time: 1.5 minutes. This resolves the historical arc and returns to the course project.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), conclusion of “The Evolution of Comparative Politics.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Context before design
Ishiyama organizes the book in two stages:


The political “soil”

Historical development
Economy
Political culture and identity
Social structure
International environment


Institutional choices

Electoral system
Executive and legislature
Courts
Federalism and local authority
Interactions among the rules



Design cannot compensate automatically for hostile contextual conditions.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Explain why the course studies context before institutional options.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “The Plan of this Book.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Your team’s comparative logic
Every team should eventually complete this sentence:

Because our focal country and shadow comparator are similar on [background conditions] but differ on [key factor or outcome], their comparison helps us evaluate the claim that [cause] conditions [outcome].


Then add:

The comparison cannot rule out [rival explanation], so we will seek additional evidence from [source or case].


Suggested time: 3 minutes. Give students 60 seconds to draft a version with one of the course pairings, then hear two examples.
[Sources] - Instructor application of Ishiyama’s comparative-method framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Five ideas to carry forward

Comparative politics is a subject and method.
Its central challenge is many explanations, few cases.
MSSD and MDSD create leverage through case selection.
The field repeatedly negotiates values, evidence, and application.
Institutional design works only when evaluated in context.



The standard for this course: make a clear claim, show comparative evidence, and state the limits of the inference.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Use as a retrieval check: hide the body and ask students to name the five ideas first.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Exit question

What makes a comparison persuasive rather than merely interesting?


Submit three sentences:

one claim about a political outcome;
one case pairing that could evaluate it; and
one rival explanation the pairing cannot eliminate.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Collect in Teams or use as the bridge to the claim–evidence map assignment.
[Sources] - Instructor synthesis based on Ishiyama (2012), Introduction.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Why did some states enter the twentieth century with durable democratic institutions while others remained authoritarian or experienced democratic breakdown?


Two readings give us different parts of an answer:

Ishiyama offers a historical explanation across six countries
Lijphart shows how to evaluate comparisons when cases are few and causes are many


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 2. - Lijphart, “Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method” (1971), pp. 682–693.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Distinguish a democratic threshold from degrees of polyarchy
Explain Ishiyama’s three historical conditions for democratization
Compare the six country trajectories using common questions
Diagnose the “many variables, small number of cases” problem
Turn a historical narrative into a testable comparative claim

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Opening comparison


Britain

Parliament constrained the Crown before industrialization
Landed elites became commercially oriented
Political inclusion widened gradually


Russia

Autocracy remained dominant
Serfdom and elite dependence persisted
Reform arrived late and was reversed




Cold-call question: Which difference looks most causally important, and what evidence would change your mind?


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, country discussions of Britain and Russia.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: why did wool matter?
Rising Mediterranean demand for English wool changed English politics. Through what mechanism?

Wool revenue let the Crown govern without summoning Parliament
Wool needs much land and little labour, so landlords enclosed the commons
Wool profits paid for the standing army the Stuarts wanted
The wool trade imported Continental ideas about representation



The second. The asymmetry is the whole mechanism: land mattered, labour did not — so the peasantry was displaced and the nobility became commercial.


[Key] The second. This separates students who followed the causal chain from those who retain only “wool was important.”
The first option inverts the political outcome — in England the Crown lost that struggle. The third attaches real Stuart-era material to the wrong mechanism. Both are plausible enough to be worth naming aloud.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: The outcome to explain

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Democracy has more than one definition
text:
Democracy has more than one definition


Schumpeter
Democracy is a method for selecting leaders through a competitive struggle for votes.
This is a narrow, procedural definition.

Held
Democracy requires political equality among members of the political community.
This is a more demanding standard.


The definition determines which cases count as democratic.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of Schumpeter and Held.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Dahl’s polyarchy
Dahl treats democracy as an ideal and uses polyarchy for real political systems.


Competition

Elected officials
Free and fair elections
Freedom of expression
Alternative information
Independent associations


Participation

Broad suffrage
Broad eligibility for office
Equal consideration of preferences



Countries may improve on one dimension without improving equally on the other.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, summary of Dahl (1989).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A democratic threshold
For the study of transitions, Ishiyama uses four minimum components drawn from Linz and Stepan and from Rose, Mishler, and Haerpfer.







Component
Diagnostic question




Rule of law
Are rulers bound by law?


Civil society
Can groups organize independently of the state?


Free and fair elections
Is there meaningful competition for office?


Accountability
Must governing officials answer for their actions?




No single component is sufficient. The combination identifies whether a regime has crossed a democratic threshold.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of the minimal definition of democracy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two measures answer different questions








Concept
What it measures
Best question




Minimal democracy
A categorical threshold
Has the regime become democratic?


Polyarchy
Degrees of competition and participation
How democratic is the regime?





Democratization first establishes the minimum institutions, then can deepen competition and participation.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: why does Dahl need a second word?
text:
Note: why does Dahl need a second word?
Dahl reserves democracy for an ideal type and calls real systems polyarchies. Why?

Because existing democracies differ from one another
Because no actual system fully approximates the ideal
Because the term applies only after a completed transition



The second. The ideal is a standard, not a description — so every real case falls short of it, and the question becomes by how much.


[Key] The second option. The common error is the first: students who remember that polyarchies vary along competition and participation mistake a consequence of the term for its reason. The third describes the minimal-threshold approach (Linz and Stepan), not Dahl.
Ask for hands before revealing. If the room splits between one and two, that split is the teaching moment.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Ishiyama’s historical argument

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Industrialization as a political shock
Industrialization changes more than production.

New classes seek political influence
Cities and markets unsettle older hierarchies
States face demands for representation and protection
Existing institutions must absorb or repress conflict



Ishiyama treats industrialization as a storm. The outcome depends partly on the political vessel constructed before the storm arrived.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, historical approach and ship metaphor.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Sequence is the central mechanism


Before
National identity, social order, and limits on rulers develop unevenly.

During
Industrialization creates new wealth, classes, conflicts, and demands.

After
Institutions incorporate new groups, break down, or harden into authoritarian rule.


The same economic shock can therefore produce different political outcomes.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three historical conditions

Political national identity existed before industrialization
Accountability and rule of law constrained rulers before industrialization
The feudal or old social order had been transformed before industrialization



The argument is configurational. The conditions reinforce each other rather than operating as isolated causes.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, three questions organizing the six cases.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: which one is not on the list?
text:
Note: which one is not on the list?
Ishiyama organizes all six cases around three conditions established before industrialization. Which of these is not one of them?

A mass national identity
Accountability and the rule of law
The old social order swept away
An industrial working class organized into parties



The fourth. It sounds like something a chapter about industrialization ought to ask — which is exactly why it is worth naming as absent.


[Key] The fourth. Party organization of the working class is not among the three. The point is not trivia: the three conditions are all pre-industrial, and the chapter’s whole argument is that what mattered had already happened before the shock arrived. A condition defined by industrial society could not do that work.
Have them write the three down here. Round 2 asks their team to answer versions of all three about their focal country.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Political national identity
Ishiyama distinguishes cultural community from political unity.







Concept
Basis of membership




Kulturnation
Shared language, culture, religion, or ancestry


Staatsnation
Shared political institutions and a recognized political community





Cultural homogeneity does not automatically produce political integration. Japan was relatively homogeneous, yet its modern political identity had to be constructed.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of cultural and political nationhood.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Accountability before mass politics
The issue is not whether a country already had universal suffrage.
The issue is whether institutions had already established that:

Rulers could be constrained
Revenue and law required bargaining
Organized interests could act outside the state
Political conflict could occur within accepted institutions


Early accountability provided channels through which later demands could enter politics.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Transformation of the old order
A landed elite may respond to economic change in different ways.


Transformed elite

Wealth becomes commercial
Status depends less on hereditary privilege
Elites can bargain within representative institutions


Persistent old order

Land and labor remain coercively organized
Elites depend on autocratic protection
New groups threaten established privilege



The second path makes democratic inclusion more threatening to incumbent elites.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, use of Barrington Moore and the transformation of feudalism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The argument as a causal chain
text:
The argument as a causal chain








Stage
Historical question
Expected consequence




Community
Is there an accepted political nation?
Conflict stays within a shared polity


Constraint
Are rulers accountable under law?
New demands enter established channels


Social order
Has hereditary privilege been transformed?
Elites can tolerate broader participation


Industrial shock
How intense is social disruption?
Earlier arrangements face a stress test


Outcome
Are conflict and inclusion institutionalized?
Democracy, instability, or authoritarianism




[Sources] - Analytical reconstruction from Ishiyama, Chapter 2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: Six trajectories

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Britain

Political centralization and national integration developed early
The wool economy and enclosure weakened the traditional peasantry
Landed elites became commercially oriented
Parliament defeated royal absolutism and secured rule-bound bargaining
Suffrage expanded within an already accepted institutional arena



Democratization widened access to the stadium. It did not require constructing a new stadium during the crisis.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Britain section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
France

Absolutism subordinated nobles and weakened independent accountability
Labor-intensive agriculture preserved a large peasantry
The Revolution destroyed noble privilege but did not produce immediate institutional consensus
New social demands repeatedly met resistance outside stable channels
Democratic development lurched through revolution, reaction, and constitutional redesign


France shows partial preparation followed by repeated institutional rupture.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, France section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: why did French feudalism survive?
text:
Note: why did French feudalism survive?
England and France faced the same commercial opening. France did not transform. Why not?

The Revolution destroyed the nobility before commercial agriculture could develop
France entered international trade later, delaying commercial pressure
French production was labour-intensive, so landlords kept peasants rather than shedding them
There was no commercial demand for French agricultural products



The third. Viniculture and similar crops needed hands on the land. Same pressure, opposite incentive, opposite outcome.


[Key] The third. The first reverses the sequence — the Revolution came after the failure to transform, and Ishiyama is explicit that it destroyed the nobility while strengthening the peasantry. The fourth is simply false in the chapter: demand rose.
This is the pair’s payoff. Ask why the comparison is informative at all, and the answer is that the crop is the only thing that differs in the relevant respect.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
United States

Colonial assemblies established traditions of representation and accountability
The country lacked European feudalism
A unified political nation remained contested by sectional identity
Slavery sustained hereditary racial privilege in the South
Civil War settled the supremacy of the national state through violence



Institutions arrived early, but national political integration arrived late.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, United States section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Germany

Political fragmentation persisted into the nineteenth century
The Junker elite retained power in Prussia
Unification occurred through authoritarian state-building and war
Industrialization outpaced democratization
Weimar inherited deep cleavages, weak democratic commitment, war debt, and severe crisis


Rapid state formation did not produce an equally rapid democratic settlement.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Germany section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Japan

Tokugawa rule ended civil conflict but preserved decentralized feudal structures
Meiji leaders constructed political identity around loyalty to the emperor
The state directed modernization under external pressure
Old domains and military traditions were adapted rather than fully displaced
Durable democracy followed defeat and postwar institutional reconstruction


Japan separates cultural homogeneity from democratic political integration.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Japan section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Russia

Empire preceded a distinct modern national political community
Loyalty centered on the Tsar and the state
Autocracy destroyed or subordinated alternative centers of power
Serfdom and a dependent nobility persisted
Reform after 1905 left the Tsar’s veto and dissolution powers intact
War and state collapse opened the path to revolution rather than democracy



Russia is Ishiyama’s sharpest contrast with Britain across all three historical conditions.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Russia section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Six cases on common dimensions











Case
Political identity before industrialization
Accountability before industrialization
Transformation of old order
Broad trajectory




Britain
Strong
Strong
Extensive
Gradual inclusion


France
Partial
Weak
Partial
Repeated rupture


United States
Contested
Strong
Mixed because of slavery
Integration through civil war


Germany
Weak
Weak
Uneven
Authoritarian unification, fragile democracy


Japan
Constructed from above
Weak
Partial
State-led modernization, postwar democracy


Russia
Imperial loyalty
Very weak
Minimal
Autocracy, revolution





[Sources] - Synthesis of Ishiyama, Chapter 2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Paired contrast: Britain and France
Both countries experienced commercial change, state formation, and class conflict.







Similar background
Critical difference




Early European states
Parliament constrained the English Crown, while French absolutism prevailed


Powerful landed elites
English elites commercialized more fully, while French landlords retained peasant labor


Industrial and urban pressures
Britain incorporated groups gradually, while France repeatedly rebuilt institutions




This pairing directs attention to accountability and elite transformation.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Paired contrast: United States and Germany
text:
Paired contrast: United States and Germany
Both were late projects of national political integration with strong regional divisions.







United States
Germany




Representative institutions preceded full national integration
Authoritarian unification preceded national democratic integration


No European feudal order, but slavery preserved hereditary privilege
Junker privilege persisted within the new state


Civil war consolidated national authority
External war consolidated an authoritarian empire




Similar problems of unity were processed through different institutions.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Paired contrast: Japan and Russia
Both pursued state-led modernization under autocratic authority.

Political identity centered on personal loyalty to the sovereign
Bureaucratic states promoted rapid economic and military change
Older social and military hierarchies persisted
Independent civil society and accountable institutions remained weak



The comparison suggests that modernization alone does not generate democracy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: Lijphart’s design audit

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four ways to study politics








Method
Cases
Control strategy




Experimental
Designed observations
Random assignment or direct manipulation


Statistical
Many
Estimate relationships while controlling for alternatives


Comparative
Few
Select and compare cases to approximate control


Case study
One
Generate, probe, confirm, or challenge theoretical claims





For Lijphart, the comparative method follows the same logic of control as statistical analysis, but with too few cases for conventional statistical control.


[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 682–685.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The central comparative problem

Many plausible explanatory variables, but only a small number of cases.


In Ishiyama’s cases, democratic outcomes may reflect several factors at once.



National identity
Accountability
Agrarian class structure
Timing of industrialization



War and defeat
Religion
State capacity
International intervention




If several causes change together, a comparison cannot easily isolate one effect.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 685–686. - Application to Ishiyama, Chapter 2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four methods, one axis






Figure 1: Lijphart’s four basic methods, arranged by how many cases they work with and how each achieves control. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Lijphart (1971), pp. 682–685.
The figure is clickable — it opens full screen, which is worth doing when you walk the four boxes.
Two things to say aloud. First, the comparative method is one of the basic scientific methods, not the scientific method — Lijphart is explicitly narrower than Lasswell and Almond, who treat comparison and science as the same thing. Second, the orange box at the bottom is the sentence students most often get wrong on assessment.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: what separates comparative from statistical?
text:
Note: what separates comparative from statistical?
Lijphart says the comparative method resembles the statistical method in every respect but one. Which one?

The comparative method discovers relationships; the statistical method only measures them
Its cases are too few to permit control through partial correlations
It achieves control by deliberate randomization
It is a narrow technique, while the statistical method is a general strategy



The second — and Lijphart goes further. There is no clear dividing line between them: the difference depends entirely on the number of cases.


[Key] The second. The first inverts Lijphart’s own distinction — he insists the comparative method is a method of discovering relationships among variables and is not a method of measurement. The third describes the experimental method; randomization is precisely what nobody can do to countries.
The payoff line: if the only difference is N, then “qualitative versus quantitative” is a difference of degree, not of kind — and the same standards of inference apply to both.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Lijphart’s four responses







Response
Practical move




Increase cases
Add countries, regions, or historical periods


Reduce property space
Combine related categories and variables


Select comparable cases
Hold background conditions as similar as possible


Focus on key variables
Prefer a parsimonious explanation




Each response improves leverage, but each also creates tradeoffs.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 686–690.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
How Ishiyama addresses small N







Lijphart’s response
Ishiyama’s design




Increase cases
Uses six national histories rather than one


Reduce property space
Organizes diverse histories around three conditions


Select comparable cases
Builds paired contrasts with partly shared contexts


Focus on key variables
Emphasizes sequence before industrialization





The chapter gains clarity by simplifying history. That same simplification creates questions about omitted causes and scope.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Comparable means comparable for a question
text:
Comparable means comparable for a question
Cases do not need to be identical.
They need to be similar on factors treated as controls and different on the factor believed to matter.



Stronger pairing
Britain and France for early state development, agrarian change, and constraints on rulers.

Harder pairing
Britain and Japan when geography, external pressure, timing, and institutional inheritance all differ.



Comparability is produced by the research question and the design.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 687–690.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What “comparable” looks like






Figure 2: Comparable cases are alike on everything treated as a control and unlike on the suspected cause and the outcome. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Lijphart (1971), pp. 687–690.
This is the figure to leave on screen while teams talk. It is the logic of their own pairing: the dossier chose two countries precisely so that the green rows hold and the orange rows move.
If a team cannot name what its green rows are, it does not yet have a controlled comparison — it has two countries.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: what makes two cases comparable?
text:
Note: what makes two cases comparable?

Similar in as many respects as possible, including the variables you want to relate
Drawn from the same region, since areas supply natural controls
Similar on many characteristics treated as constants, but different on the variables you want to relate
Different in as many respects as possible, so a shared outcome must have a common cause



The third. Cases that are similar in every respect would leave nothing to explain.


[Key] The third. The first is the intuitive error — students hear “comparable” and think “alike in every way.” The second is the area-studies approach, which Lijphart treats as a useful aid but warns can become “a form of imprisonment.” The fourth describes a most-different design.
Say plainly: this is what Round 1 asks each team to defend, and “both are in Africa” is the answer that loses marks.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Case studies can serve different purposes
text:
Case studies can serve different purposes








Type
Role in theory




Atheoretical
Describes a case without engaging a broader proposition


Interpretive
Uses an existing theory to explain a case


Hypothesis-generating
Develops a new proposition from close study


Theory-confirming
Adds a case that fits an existing proposition


Theory-infirming
Adds a case that weakens confidence in a proposition


Deviant
Studies an unexpected case to refine the theory





Hypothesis-generating and deviant cases are especially useful for building better explanations.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 691–693.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Deviant cases refine probabilistic claims
Suppose the claim is:

Early accountability usually increases the chance of durable democratization.


A case with early accountability and democratic failure matters, but it does not automatically disprove the claim.
Questions for the deviant case:

Was accountability genuine or only formal?
Did war or state collapse overwhelm the expected effect?
Does the theory require another condition?
Is the claim limited to a particular historical scope?


[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), discussion of theory-infirming and deviant cases.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: A design audit of the chapter
text:
A design audit of the chapter


Explanatory gains

Common questions discipline six narratives
Historical sequence identifies plausible mechanisms
Paired contrasts reveal meaningful differences
Cases connect institutions to social structure


Remaining limits

Cases are concentrated in major powers
Several causes move together
Outcome categories are broad
The framework is strongly rooted in Western history



The comparison is valuable when its scope and uncertainty remain explicit.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, concluding caveats. - Lijphart (1971), comparative method limitations.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: After the six cases

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The Third Wave
Huntington coined the phrase in 1991. The wave began in the mid-1970s and gathered speed as the Cold War wound down and the Soviet Union collapsed.

Early optimism assumed that underdevelopment and other structural constraints would not impede democracy’s spread.



Haggard and Kaufman’s summary of what actually happened: the net increase in the number of democracies hid substantial churning, with a steady if small stream of reversions to authoritarian rule.


[Sources] Haggard and Kaufman (2016), Annual Review of Political Science 19: 125–144, pp. 126–127.
Connect back to Ishiyama deliberately. Chapter 2 explains six cases that had already democratized by the twentieth century. Haggard and Kaufman survey what happened to everyone else, and they reach a methodological conclusion very close to Lijphart’s.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Transitions to what?
Early work treated the puzzle as the collapse of authoritarian rule — the exit of incumbents, capped by founding elections.

But many Third Wave transitions produced regimes that fell short of democracy on any broader definition:

Competitive authoritarian (Levitsky and Way) · illiberal · electoral authoritarian · hybrid

Elections held, limited political space, but a playing field the incumbent defines.



These are not way stations. A growing recognition is that competitive authoritarianism may be a persistent equilibrium in its own right.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
When two datasets disagree






Figure 3: Cheibub et al. and the Polity Project code the same phenomenon and agree on barely half of it. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Haggard and Kaufman (2016), p. 128.
This is the slide to linger on, because it is the dossier lesson in miniature. Every team’s dossier reports figures that disagree with each other, and every team will be tempted to pick the flattering one.
The honest move is the one Haggard and Kaufman make: say which measure you used, say why, and say what changes if you had used the other.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Structure returned, but without mechanisms
As optimism about “crafting” democracy ebbed, structural theories came back: level of development, inequality, resource endowments, ethnic and religious heterogeneity.

But the findings are mixed almost everywhere you look:







Structural claim
What the evidence does




Inequality drives transitions
Boix finds support; Houle, Ahlquist and Wibbels, and Haggard and Kaufman find no significant relationship


Resource wealth blocks democracy
Contested; Haber and Menaldo find no relationship, and selection bias cuts against the standard test


Ethnic fragmentation destabilizes democracy
Few tests exist; Fish and Brooks, and Fish and Kroenig, find effects disappear with development






Haggard and Kaufman’s diagnosis: the enduring weakness of these theories is inattention to the mechanisms linking structure to regime change.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Development: which question?


Transitions
Does development cause authoritarian regimes to democratize?
Contested. Przeworski et al. argued it does not; Boix and Stokes challenged them using a longer time frame.

Consolidation
Does development help democracies survive?
Much stronger consensus. Przeworski et al.: no democracy had ever reverted above a per capita income of $6,055 — Argentina’s level in 1975.



Same variable, two questions, two very different states of knowledge. Which question you ask decides what the literature can tell you.


[Sources] Haggard and Kaufman (2016), p. 129. Boix shows the result is stronger still in the post–Cold War period.
Worth adding: a number of poor democracies have nonetheless survived a long time — Benin since 1991, Mongolia since 1992, Ghana since 1993, Moldova since 1993. The threshold is a regularity, not a law.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
No taproot

Haggard and Kaufman’s central methodological claim: the quest for an overarching theory of democratization — a taproot — is probably misguided.


Even well-supported cross-national generalizations must accommodate numerous anomalies. Their prescription:

Combinations of causal factors rather than single causes
Alternative pathways to the same outcome
Equifinality — different routes, same destination




Notice what this is not. It is not a call for more data. It is a claim that the assumption of one causal path is the problem.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The same conclusion, from two directions
text:
The same conclusion, from two directions


Lijphart, 1971
Too many variables, too few cases. Control by selecting cases; be modest about what one comparison can establish.

Haggard and Kaufman, 2016
Large-N work yields anomalies. Look for combinations, pathways, equifinality; use qualitative work on necessary and sufficient conditions.



Forty-five years apart, working from opposite ends of the N, and they arrive at the same place: a single general law of democratization is not what this field is going to produce.


This is the slide that justifies the course design. The team project asks for a diagnosis of one country against one comparator — not a theory of democratization. Haggard and Kaufman are the reason that is the right ambition rather than a modest one.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: what follows from “no taproot”?
Haggard and Kaufman argue the search for an overarching theory is misguided. What do they conclude the field should do?

Build larger cross-national datasets, since samples are too small to detect the true effect
Attend to combinations of causal factors, alternative pathways, and equifinality
Move to formal models that specify precise conditions
Agree on one measure of democracy, since disagreement is mostly definitional



The second. More data would not help if the problem is the assumption of a single path.


[Key] The second. The first is the instinct almost everyone has — anomalies mean underpowered tests — and it is exactly what they argue against.
The fourth is tempting after the measurement slide. Note the difference: they do think measurement matters a great deal, but they never suggest one agreed measure would dissolve the theoretical problem.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: development and democracy
On development, where is the consensus in the literature stronger?

Transitions — development reliably causes authoritarian regimes to democratize
Consolidation — development is associated with democracies surviving
Neither, since the correlation disappears once region is controlled
Resource wealth specifically, now agreed to be the decisive form of development



The second. The transition question remains contested; the survival question is where the evidence is strongest.


[Key] The second. The first states the classic modernization claim, which Haggard and Kaufman report as contested — Przeworski et al. against Boix and Stokes.
If students remember only one thing from this pair of slides, it should be that “does development cause democracy?” is two questions wearing one coat.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 6: From reading to research

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A claim-evidence map








Element
Example




Claim
Early constraints on rulers make later democratic inclusion more durable.


Mechanism
New groups can pursue demands through accepted institutions rather than extra-institutional conflict.


Evidence for
Britain had parliamentary constraint before industrialization and expanded participation gradually.


Comparative evidence
France developed under absolutism and repeatedly experienced rupture during inclusion.


Rival explanation
Different agrarian class structures, not accountability, drove the contrast.


Discriminating evidence
Compare cases with similar agrarian structures but different levels of early accountability.


Scope
European states undergoing early industrialization.





[Sources] - Example synthesized from Ishiyama, Chapter 2, using Lijphart’s logic of control.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Team comparison workshop
For the focal country and shadow comparator:

Record each country’s value on Ishiyama’s three historical conditions
Identify one outcome that differs between the countries
State one causal claim that could explain the difference
Name one rival explanation
Identify evidence that would distinguish the two explanations



The goal is not to find two identical countries. The goal is to make the basis of comparison explicit.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A stronger team presentation
An effective weekly presentation includes:

One comparative puzzle
One explicit causal claim
Evidence from both countries
One rival explanation
One limitation of the comparison
One question for the class


The presenters defend the comparison. The class serves as the design review panel.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
History constrains without determining
Ishiyama rejects a mechanical reading of the argument.

Long-term structures shape the options available to leaders
Critical moments still involve political choices
Institutions can redirect inherited conflict
External shocks can alter trajectories



Historical conditions change probabilities. They do not write an unavoidable political future.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, conclusion and discussion of critical choices.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: constraint or destiny?
Ishiyama cites Sartori to warn against one reading of the six cases. Which?

Historical factors describe background conditions but explain nothing
Democracy was the product of human choices at critical moments, though choices were constrained
Every case is unique, so comparison cannot support generalization
Institutions matter only after a country has crossed the democratic threshold



The second. Democracy “did not just happen, nor was it predetermined by history or culture” — but leaders cannot engineer it where no social or economic base supports it.


[Key] The second. The first overstates: Ishiyama says historical factors are useful for describing background conditions, just not determinative. The third is the opposite of the chapter’s purpose.
This is the one to spend a minute on. If history determined outcomes there would be nothing for a constitutional engineer to do, and the team paper would be incoherent. A student who misses this has not yet understood what they are writing in December.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Core takeaways

Definitions determine the outcome we are trying to explain
Ishiyama emphasizes the sequence of identity, accountability, and social transformation before industrialization
The six histories become comparable only when organized by common questions
Lijphart identifies the central weakness of the design: many causes and few cases
Pairing, parsimony, rival explanations, and deviant cases can strengthen comparative inference

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

When do identities become political — and does culture explain anything that economics has not already explained?


Chapter 3 left political culture sitting as the intervening step between economic change and political change. Chapter 4 asks whether it can carry that weight, or whether it is a residual we reach for when structure runs out.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 4, pp. 89–117.
Two halves to the chapter, and they are easy to lose track of. The first half is a concept under attack: political culture as attitudes, then three waves of criticism, then a renaissance. The second half is ethnicity and nationalism, which arrives because by the era of multiculturalism “culture” had come to be used interchangeably with ethnicity.
Keep the stakes in view: both halves end up at the same question, which is whether a society’s identities make democracy harder.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class you should be able to:

State Almond and Verba’s definition of political culture and place a country in Table 4.1
Say what the civic culture is a mix of, and why the mix matters more than any single type
Rehearse the three criticisms — definition, explanatory power, and production — and the best answer to each
Explain post-materialism, how it is measured, and what the measurement critique shows
Distinguish primordial from constructivist accounts of ethnicity
Use Greenfeld’s two dimensions to classify a nationalism
Separate fractionalization from polarization in the diversity-and-democracy debate
Name nationalism’s two core principles, and say why neither of them mentions ethnicity

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: What is political culture?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Older than political science
Political culture is, at bottom, “the basic values, ideas, beliefs, attitudes, and orientations about politics” — what is right and wrong, acceptable and unacceptable, in political life.

Max Weber argued the values of Protestantism — hard work, honesty, seriousness, monetary thrift and efficiency — were especially conducive to the accumulation of capital, and so to capitalism and eventually democracy.

A comparative study: Buddhism, Catholicism, Confucianism, Islam
Other societies had some of these values; none had them all


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 89–90; Weber on the Protestant ethic.
The move that matters for us is that Weber’s claim was comparative in structure — he did not study Protestantism alone, he studied it against four alternatives. That is the standard the next generation failed to meet.
Weber’s extra wrinkle: accumulating wealth through commerce and usury — previously frowned on by the Catholic Church — came to signify that one was viewed favourably in the eyes of God.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Landes: the valuing of science
David Landes (1998) asks why industrialization came first to northern Europe — England, Germany, the Netherlands, Scandinavia.
His answer is cultural, but a different culture:

A valuing of science
Respect for autonomous intellectual inquiry
An emphasis on empiricism — itself growing out of the Protestant emphasis on the observable as proof of God’s favour



These values drove scientific and technological innovation from the Renaissance onward, laying the intellectual groundwork for the Industrial Revolution.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The war that made the field — and its flaw
text:
The war that made the field — and its flaw
As Wiarda (1999) notes, political culture studies were boosted by World War II.

Ruth Benedict (1934; The Chrysanthemum and the Sword, 1954)
Margaret Mead (1964)
Nathan Leites (1951)


Several were commissioned by the US government — first against Japan, then against the Soviet Union.



They did study attitudes toward power, hierarchy and duty. But they were non-comparative, single-country studies, emphasizing what was unique to each culture — which gave political scientists no general method.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 90.
This is a methodological point disguised as a history lesson, and it is worth naming as such in class — it is exactly Lijphart’s complaint from Session 1. A rich single-country description is not an explanation, because nothing varies.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The breakthrough: The Civic Culture (1963)
Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba did two things the anthropologists had not.

Built a framework for systematic comparison across countries, instead of letting patterns “emerge”
Answered the question the earlier literature had dodged: beliefs and attitudes about what?



Political culture is “a set of specifically political orientations — attitudes toward the political system and its part and attitudes towards the role of the self in the system.”
[Almond and Verba 1963, p. 12]


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 90–91; Almond and Verba (1963, p. 12).
Two components in that definition, and the whole chapter turns on them: orientations (the psychological side) and objects (what the orientations are about). The objects are the parts of the political system as the structural-functionalist approach of Chapter 1 identified them — input processes, output processes, structures of the system.
Flag now, pay off later: the clause “the role of the self in the system” is precisely what Lijphart will call concept stretching.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: how do Almond and Verba define it?
text:
Check: how do Almond and Verba define it?
Almond and Verba define a political culture as:

The totality of ideas and attitudes towards authority, discipline, governmental responsibilities and entitlements
A set of specifically political orientations — attitudes toward the political system and its parts, and attitudes towards the role of the self in the system
A system of common basic values that help shape the behavior of the people in a given society
The images, symbols, myths and traditions that enable people to make sense of their situation



The second. Orientations and objects — attitudes toward the system, and toward the role of the self within it.


[Key] Option 2 (Almond and Verba 1963, p. 12).
Every other option is a real definition from later in this chapter — option 1 is Robertson (1985), option 3 is Inglehart (1997), option 4 is Welch (1993). Say that out loud, because it is the point: the definitions arrive in sequence, each displacing the last, and a student who cannot order them has read the chapter as a list of names.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three orientations







Cognitive
Knowledge of and belief about the political system, its roles, the incumbents of those roles, inputs and outputs


Affective
Feelings about the political system, its roles, personnel and performance


Evaluational
Judgments and opinions about political objects — typically combining value judgments or feelings with information





Note that evaluation is not a separate kind of thing but a combination: feeling plus information.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: which three orientations?
Almond and Verba identify three kinds of psychological orientation. They are:

Traditional, transitional, and modern
Parochial, subject, and participant
Cognitive, affective, and evaluational
Individual, collective, and national



Cognitive, affective, evaluational. Parochial, subject and participant are the three types, not the three orientations — the types are what you get when the orientations are pointed at the four system dimensions.


[Key] Option 3. Option 2 is the trap and it is worth dwelling on, because the confusion is not trivial: a student who cannot separate orientations from types cannot read Table 4.1 at all.
Put it as a sequence on the board — three orientations, four objects, three named types — and the architecture of the whole first half becomes visible.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four system dimensions
Each of the three orientations can be directed at four different objects:

The system as a whole — constitutional characteristics, political structures
The policy process — input objects, e.g. interest groups, parties
Policy enforcement — how policy is implemented; output objects
The self — does the individual perceive themselves as a member of the system, with a positive impact on it?



Collapse dimensions 2, 3 and 4 into a plus or a minus and you get the three political culture types.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 91–92.
Students read Table 4.1 as arbitrary unless they see that it is generated by this list. Build it on the board: system, input, output, self — four columns, and only three of the sixteen logical combinations get names.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Table 4.1 · Political culture types

Ishiyama, Table 4.1
