Read down the input and self columns. That is where the three types actually differ — everyone past the parochial stage notices the state and takes its benefits.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, Table 4.1, after Almond and Verba (1963).
Worth saying out loud: the subject row is the interesting one, because it is positive on the system and on outputs but negative on inputs and self. That is a citizen who consumes government and does not make it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Parochial
Citizens are only remotely aware of a central government, and live their lives regardless of what the state decides.

Know little or nothing of the system, its parts, its processes
Do not believe they should participate
Do not expect to be beneficiaries of policy
See no role for the self



The old Russian peasant proverb: “God is high above and the Tsar is far away.”



Predominates in relatively poor, underdeveloped, agrarian societies where orientations are local rather than national — but parochials can be found in any society.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what marks a parochial culture?
text:
Check: what marks a parochial culture?
In a parochial political culture, citizens:

Know the system well and believe they should participate in it
Are only remotely aware of a central government and live their lives regardless of what the state decides
Accept the benefits of government policy but do not believe they can influence it
Reject the legitimacy of the state and organize to overthrow it



Remotely aware, and indifferent. The Tsar is far away — and the third option is the subject, not the parochial.


[Key] Option 2. Option 3 is the one that costs points, because both parochials and subjects are non-participants and students stop reading once they see “do not believe they can influence it.”
The discriminating question is about outputs: a subject consumes what the state produces; a parochial does not expect to be a beneficiary of policy at all.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Subject
People know the system and something of how it works, but see themselves as subjects to authority.

Positively oriented to outputs — employment, education, healthcare — which they are quite willing to consume
Not oriented to inputs; no belief in a role for the self
Do not think they can or should articulate interests, aggregate them, or enter the policy process



Dominant in modern authoritarian states — the Soviet Union, Nazi Germany — where citizen activities are defined as duties rather than rights, and where the regime rests on performance legitimacy: as long as the outputs keep coming, people stay loyal.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 92–93.
The performance-legitimacy point is the one with the most mileage for their dossiers. It is also the bridge to Chapter 3: a subject culture plus a growth record is a stable authoritarianism, and a subject culture plus a recession is a crisis.
Such regimes often ground their right to rule in some ubiquitous “law of history” that only the political elite can interpret.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: what is performance legitimacy?
Regimes resting on a subject political culture often reinforce their right to rule through performance legitimacy, which means:

Leaders must demonstrate personal competence before taking office
As long as the outputs keep being produced, people will remain loyal to the system
Legitimacy is earned through competitive elections held at regular intervals
Officials are evaluated by an independent bureaucracy against published standards



Outputs buy loyalty. A subject culture plus a growth record is a stable authoritarianism — and the same culture plus a recession is a crisis.


[Key] Option 2.
The sentence to add after revealing it: such regimes often ground their right to rule in some ubiquitous “law of history” that only the political elite can interpret. Ideology supplies the story; performance supplies the evidence.
This is the slide with the most dossier mileage in Part 1, and it is the bridge back to Chapter 3.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Participant
Individuals who know a great deal about the system, are positively oriented to both inputs and outputs, and believe they have a positive role to play.

They want to participate and to receive the benefits of policy
Found in modern, developed, wealthy societies with high mass literacy and education



Almond and Verba’s 1963 expectation: as a result of modernization, the world could be expected to become more participant.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 93.
That last sentence is modernization theory from Chapter 3, restated at the level of attitudes. Ask whether the sixty years since have borne it out — and what evidence would settle it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Ideal types, individually held, nationally mixed
text:
Ideal types, individually held, nationally mixed
Three things Almond and Verba insist on, all of which students skip:

These are ideal types — idealized characterizations, not descriptions of real societies
The attitudes are held at the individual level
Aggregated to the nation, every country is a mix of all three



So the comparative question is never “which type is this country.” It is what is the relative mix — in some the parochial impulse predominates, in others the participant.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The civic culture is a mix, not a maximum
text:
The civic culture is a mix, not a maximum

The mix that best supports stable democracy — the civic culture — is a majority of participants, tempered by a significant minority of subjects and some parochials.


From interviews with over 5,000 people across five countries, conducted over five years:

Great Britain and the United States — highest proportion of participants
Germany and Italy — highest proportion of subjects, consistent with their recent emergence from totalitarianism
Mexico — least democratic, greatest number of subjects and parochials


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 93–94; Almond and Verba (1963).
Do not let the headline finding pass without the footnote: Almond and Verba expressed concern that the proportion of participants in the United States was too high, and presented a destabilizing element in American politics. That is counter-intuitive enough to be memorable, and it is the whole reason the civic culture is defined as a tempered mix rather than a maximum.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what is the civic culture?
text:
Check: what is the civic culture?
Almond and Verba’s civic culture consists of:

Participants only
A majority of participants, tempered by some subjects and parochials
An equal share of all three types
A majority of subjects with a participant elite



A majority of participants, tempered by a significant minority of subjects and some parochials. Too many participants was itself a destabilizing element — which is why the answer is a mix and not a maximum.


[Key] Option 2. “Participants only” is the trap, because it is what the word “civic” suggests and what students assume the theory must want.
If someone picks option 1, the follow-up question is: what would a polity of nothing but participants look like? Almond and Verba’s worry was overload — every demand pressed at once, with nobody willing to defer.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Elazar: three American political cultures
Daniel Elazar (1972, 1994) applies the same logic inside one country, focusing on how people perceive the role of government.







Moral
Social concerns outweigh the individual; government a positive force; the commonwealth conception; politics as one of the great activities of man in search of the good society; issues matter; politicians are not to profit; more amateur participation


Individual
Government largely an impediment, to be restricted so as not to interfere with private activity; its role confined to encouraging private initiative; private concerns outweigh public


Traditional
Social and family ties prominent; emphasis on traditional hierarchies; government has a positive role but limited to maintaining the existing social order; leaders custodial rather than innovative




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 94–95; Elazar (1994, pp. 230–235).
Useful for a Texas classroom: Elazar’s own mapping puts Texas in the traditionalistic-individualistic band. Ask students which of the three they recognize in state politics, and what evidence they would cite — this is a low-stakes rehearsal of the claim-evidence map.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Three criticisms

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The three lines of attack


Definition — is the concept coherent, or stretched past usefulness?
Explanatory power — can culture be an independent variable at all?
Production — what explains where political cultures come from?



Together these drove the concept into decline. Each one also produced the repair that brought it back.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Criticism 1: the concept is stretched
Arend Lijphart (1980) is sympathetic — political culture is a powerful explanatory variable — but argues Almond and Verba stretched it.

Beyond orientations toward the political system, into general social and personal relations
Specifically, “the role of the self in the system”
The result is an unnecessary vagueness



His repair: focus entirely on how politics is conducted, not on feelings about the self and how the self interacts with others.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 95–96; Lijphart (1980).
Same Lijphart as Session 1, and the same instinct: a concept that travels too far stops discriminating between cases. Worth naming the continuity explicitly — students treat the Lijphart of the comparative method and the Lijphart of consociationalism as two different people.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Lijphart’s replacement: how decisions get made
text:
Lijphart’s replacement: how decisions get made







Consensual
Political decisions should maximize the number of points of view represented; consensus among them should be achieved; societal differences are tolerated


Conflictual / adversarial
Politics painted in stark contrasts — right and wrong — with emphasis on the triumph of one side over the other




For Lijphart (1999), consensual political culture produces “kinder and gentler” policies than majoritarian political cultures.



And the link runs both ways: consensual culture goes with consensual institutions, adversarial culture with majoritarian institutions.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 96; Lijphart (1999, p. 305).
Hold this slide for Session 9 — Lijphart’s “Constitutional Choices for New Democracies” is the November 5 article, and this is its cultural premise.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Richardson: fair share and fair play
text:
Richardson: fair share and fair play
Bradley Richardson (1984), on Japanese political culture, draws the same contrast at the level of what citizens think fairness is.







Fair share (consensual)
What matters is that all share equally in the outcome


Fair play (adversarial)
No matter the outcome, if the game was played fairly the result is legitimate





This is a usable test. Ask of any political system: when people call an outcome unjust, are they objecting to the distribution or to the procedure?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The European redefinitions
Scholars took a broader view: political culture as what lets people make sense of politics, not as attitudes toward one particular system.







Elkins & Simeon (1979)
A set of assumptions; a “mind set” that limits attention to less than the full range of logically possible behaviours, problems and solutions


Robertson (1985)
“The totality of ideas and attitudes towards authority, discipline, governmental responsibilities and entitlements”


Rose (1980)
Sets of “values, beliefs and emotions,” taken for granted, which “give meaning to politics”


Kavanagh (1985)
Disposes members to regard certain political behaviour and institutions as “normal” and others as “abnormal”


Topf (1989)
Attitudes as “expressions of values, or better, of positions in the moral order, constitutive of the political culture”


Welch (1993)
Not assumptions but resources — images, symbols, myths, traditions people draw on to make sense of their predicament




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 96–98.
Don’t drill the names. Drill the shift: from attitudes about a system to the equipment people use to interpret any system. The second version is detachable from institutions, which is what the critics demanded — and it is also vaguer, which is what Lijphart warned about. The field traded one problem for the other.
The Elkins and Simeon formulation is the one to keep: choices from a restricted set “remain below the threshold of consciousness, because they seldom encounter individuals who take for granted quite different assumptions” (1979, p. 128).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Criticism 2: is culture a cause or a result?
text:
Criticism 2: is culture a cause or a result?
Carole Pateman (1971): if political orientations are an integral part of the political system, attitudes can exist only in relation to a specific set of institutions.


Then political culture cannot be an independent variable, because it cannot be separated from the institutional context in which it exists.



Brian Barry goes further. Political culture is merely “reasonable expectations founded on common experience” of the existing system:

“Obviously, if this interpretation is correct, there are no grounds for saying that the correlation arises from the conduciveness of the ‘civic culture’ to ‘democracy’, but rather for the unexciting conclusion that ‘democracy’ produces the ‘civic culture’.”
[Barry 1978, pp. 51–52]


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 98–99; Barry (1978, pp. 51–52); Pateman (1971, 1980).
This is the single most transferable idea in the chapter: reverse causation. Name it as such.
Marxist critics such as Jerzy Wiatr (1980) point in the same direction, to the causal influence of social and economic realities on political culture. Pateman adds that the argument “neglects the association between class and participation and implies that social status is irrelevant” (1980, p. 84).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: Barry’s objection
Barry’s claim that “democracy produces the civic culture” is best described as:

A measurement-validity problem
A reverse-causation problem
A selection-bias problem
A concept-stretching problem



Reverse causation. The correlation is not in dispute — what is in dispute is which way the arrow points, and Barry argues the civic culture is the residue of living under democracy rather than its cause.


[Key] Option 2. Concept stretching is Lijphart’s separate objection, and measurement validity is the later Clarke et al. critique of Inglehart’s index — both appear in this chapter, which is why they make good distractors.
Push it one step: what evidence would separate the two stories? Over-time data on attitudes in countries that democratize later, which is exactly the design the World Values Survey eventually made possible.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Lijphart’s defence, and a smaller claim
text:
Lijphart’s defence, and a smaller claim
Lijphart (1980) replies that the question is wrongly posed: it is a mistake to think of culture and structure in either/or terms.

Structures clearly affect political culture
Culture clearly affects which structures emerge
They are inherently linked and occur simultaneously


Elkins and Simeon (1979) offer the more modest repair: most studies fail to control for other factors.

Political culture should not be the explanation of first resort but of last resort — what social, economic and political structures cannot explain. It is the variation in the dependent variable that structural factors leave over.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 99–100.
The last-resort rule is methodologically respectable and intellectually deflating at once, and it is worth putting that tension to the class. It does protect against lazy culturalism. It also guarantees that culture can never be tested directly, only credited with a residual.
For their dossiers, the rule is a discipline: a team that reaches for “the political culture there is different” before exhausting institutional and economic explanations has skipped the work.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: the explanation of last resort
text:
Check: the explanation of last resort
Elkins and Simeon argue political culture should be the explanation of “last resort.” By this they mean:

Political culture explains more than any structural variable, so it should be tested first
Political culture should be invoked only for what social, economic and political structures cannot explain
Cultural explanations are valid only where no survey data exist
Political culture matters only once a country has already become democratic



Only for the residual. Culture is the variation structure leaves over — which protects against lazy culturalism, and also means culture can never be tested directly.


[Key] Option 2. Option 1 inverts the rule and will catch anyone who reads “last resort” as a compliment rather than a demotion.
Put the tension to the class rather than resolving it. The rule is methodologically respectable and intellectually deflating at once: it is a good discipline and a guarantee that the concept can only ever be credited with a remainder.
For the dossiers it is a checklist item — a team reaching for “the political culture there is different” before exhausting institutions and economics has skipped the work.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Criticism 3: where do political cultures come from?
text:
Criticism 3: where do political cultures come from?
Almond and Verba show correlations between attitudes and educational attainment, implying political culture is produced by individuals and institutions together.


But they never explain how, beyond invoking political socialization
And Pateman (1980): socialization only takes an active role if there are tensions between people’s independently generated orientations and how the system actually works




Definition problems, plus the independence problem, plus no account of production — together these produced a decline in interest in the concept in comparative politics.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: The renaissance

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Why the concept came back
At the end of the 1980s, renewed interest in the United States — Europe had never abandoned it.

Real-world puzzles no structural account could handle: radical Islamic fundamentalism; the extraordinary modernization of several East Asian countries
The collapse of the Soviet Union and of communism in Central and Eastern Europe — how had changing political cultures brought communism down?
Consolidation: the congruence of culture with institutions as a prerequisite for new democracies (Linz and Stepan 1996; Rose, Mishler and Haerpfer 1998; Diamond 1999)



Putnam (1993), Making Democracy Work, on the republican virtues — civic community, tolerance, cooperation, solidarity.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 100–101.
Note the pattern, because it recurs in the discipline: a concept returns not because its logical problems were solved but because events arrived that rival concepts could not explain.
Inglehart’s own definition is the detached one: culture is “a system of common basic values that help shape the behavior of the people in a given society” (1997, p. 217) — values and attitudes independent of particular political structures.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Inglehart: post-materialism
As in Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, individuals pursue goals in hierarchical order — material needs first, non-material needs as material ones are satisfied.








Scarcity
Emphasis on economic growth and security — strong national defence, “law and order”


Affluence
Shift to personal freedom, political participation, quality of life, a clean environment






And not a passing mood: through socialization, post-material orientations transfer to subsequent generations and become a stable value system rather than a volatile attitude.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what is post-materialism built on?
text:
Check: what is post-materialism built on?
Inglehart’s theory of post-materialism is built on an analogy with:

Weber’s distinction between traditional and rational-legal authority
Maslow’s hierarchy of human needs
Durkheim’s account of the division of labour
Parsons’s traditional and modern ideal types



Maslow. Goals are pursued in hierarchical order — material needs first, non-material needs once the material ones are met.


[Key] Option 2. Option 1 is the sharp distractor, and deliberately so: Weber’s authority distinction is Inglehart’s other dimension — the rows of Table 4.2, two slides from now — just not the basis of post-materialism itself.
Options 3 and 4 are Chapter 4’s opening pages and Chapter 3 respectively. Students who are tracking which author belongs to which argument will clear this; students carrying a bag of names will not.
