title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The four-item index
Inglehart’s measure, built on American National Election Studies data. Respondents choose their first and then their second most desirable national goal:

Maintaining order in the nation
Giving the people more say in important political decisions
Fighting rising prices
Protecting freedom of speech



(1) and (3) → pure materialists · (2) and (4) → post-materialists
[Inglehart 1971, p. 94]



World Values Survey (2000) — highest post-materialist shares: Australia 35%, Austria 30%, Canada 29%, United States 25%.

[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 102–103; Inglehart (1971, p. 94); Inglehart et al. (2004, p. 384).
Read the four items aloud and have students answer privately before revealing the coding. Then ask what the index assumes: that items 1 and 3 are the economic-and-security pair, and 2 and 4 the autonomy pair. The critique on a later slide is an attack on exactly that assumption.
Subsequent variations appear in the General Social Survey, the World Values Survey and elsewhere.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The new values of the 1990s
By the 1990s the shift had produced a distinct set of political values:

The diminishing effectiveness and acceptability of bureaucratic authority — small is better
A growing emphasis on individual freedom and emotional experience, and the questioning of all forms of authority
The diminishing prestige of science, technology and rationality, and a re-embrace of religion



That third item is the one that generates Table 4.2: religion returning as a basis of authority cross-cuts the materialist/post-materialist axis rather than lying along it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Table 4.2 · Material versus post-material values by authority type
text:
Table 4.2 · Material versus post-material values by authority type

Ishiyama, Table 4.2








Traditional values(materialist)
Postmodern values(post-materialist)




Rational / legal / secular(emphasis on state authority)
Post-communist Eastern Europe, China, Japan (somewhat)
Northern Europe, Canada (increasingly Japan)


Traditional authority(e.g. religion)
Poland, most of the developing world
Italy, Spain, Mexico, Argentina, the US (a borderline case), Ireland




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, Table 4.2; after Weber (1947) on patterns of authority and Inglehart.
The rows come from Weber’s distinction between rational-legal and traditional bases of state authority: people obey either because it is in their self-interest to do so, or because that is how it has always been — often because authority rests on religious values. The columns are Inglehart’s value axis. Two dimensions, four cells.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Reading Table 4.2

Secular + materialist — the post-communist states, from communism’s secular legacy plus relatively lower development than the West. China likewise. Poland is the exception, where Catholicism is a powerful legitimizing force
Secular + post-materialist — most of northern Europe, Canada, and to some extent the US. Japan is a borderline case: secular, and increasingly post-materialist
Traditional + materialist — most of the developing world
Traditional + post-materialist — Catholic southern Europe, Latin America, and arguably the US, given the strong influence of religion on its politics



The payoff for democracy: where traditional authority predominates, expect a less participatory impulse — close to Almond and Verba’s subject culture. Add materialist values and you get something less than participatory democracy.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 104–105.
The US appears twice and students will object. Say why: Ishiyama treats it as a borderline case on the authority dimension precisely because religion weighs unusually heavily in American politics for a wealthy secular-legal state. A case that resists the typology is a finding, not an error.
The chapter’s own conclusion is the one to write down: economic development and post-material values may lead to democracy, but the quality of that democracy, or its type, is powerfully affected by the legacy of past authority patterns.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Postmodernization
Inglehart (1997) generalizes beyond post-materialism: western industrial democracies have entered a new phase.

“In the postmodernization phase of development, emphasis shifts from maximizing economic gains to maximizing subjective well-being.” [(p. 86)]


The post-materialist shift is “only one part of a broader shift toward postmodern values, involving changing orientations towards politics, work, family life, religion, and sexual behavior” (p. 132).



New priorities follow: environmental protection, abortion, ethnic diversity, women’s issues, gay rights [(p. 247)].


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 105–106; Inglehart (1997).
Micro-level evidence Ishiyama cites for the West: class-based cleavages have weakened (Huckfeldt and Kohfeld 1989; Ladd and Hadley 1975), and social and cultural issues have moved to the forefront of American politics ahead of bread-and-butter economics (Inglehart and Abramson 1994).
The party-level illustration is the better teaching case. Before WWII the Social Democratic/Labour Left fought over wages, the economic rights of the working classes, and ownership of the means of production. After the post-war boom came a “greening” of the European Left, accelerating in the 1990s: openness, accountability, public-private partnership, smaller government, individual rights. Ishiyama reads Blairism, and the merger that produced the Dutch GroenLinks, in this light.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The measurement critique
Critics (Flanagan 1982; Clarke and Dutt 1991; Duch and Taylor 1993, 1994) attack the four-item index itself.
Clarke et al. (1999, p. 637): substituting an unemployment statement for the standard inflation statement “has major consequences for the classification of respondents as materialist or postmaterialist.”

“When inflation is not a salient economic problem, respondents eschew the rising prices item but are forced by the format to choose one of the remaining three, none of which deals with other economic concerns they may have. Respondents who do not select the prices item have a zero probability of being classified as materialist.”



The deeper worry: post-materialism may not be a stable value set at all, but a response to conditions — post-materialist in good times, materialist in downturns or under security threat.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 106–107; Clarke et al. (1999, p. 637).
Note where this lands: back at Barry’s objection. If values track economic conditions, then culture again lacks an independent effect beyond economic and material circumstances — the same criticism made of Almond and Verba thirty years earlier.
Methodologically this is a forced-choice instrument problem, and it generalizes. Ask students what happens to any ranking scale when the item that would capture a respondent’s real concern is simply not on the list.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what is the Clarke et al. critique?
text:
Check: what is the Clarke et al. critique?
The Clarke et al. (1999) objection to Inglehart’s index is that:

The sample was unrepresentative
The forced-choice format makes classification depend on which items are offered
Post-materialism was measured in too few countries
Respondents misunderstood the question wording



The forced-choice format. Swap the inflation item for an unemployment item and respondents get reclassified — so the measure is partly an artefact of the instrument, and partly of current economic conditions.


[Key] Option 2. This item is doing double duty: it tests the chapter, and it tests whether students can tell a measurement problem from a sampling problem. Both appear in their own dossier work.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: Ethnic politics and nationalism

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Why ethnicity enters a chapter on culture
text:
Why ethnicity enters a chapter on culture
As political culture came to mean a set of values through which politics is interpreted, it moved closer to the other shortcuts people use to make sense of politics.


In the era of multiculturalism, culture became equated with ethnicity
In the US especially, multiculturalism is used interchangeably with inter-ethnic or inter-racial relations




Ishiyama’s justification is the close relationship between cultural and ethnic identities — but notice that an equation has quietly been made, and it is worth asking whether it holds.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What is “ethnicity”?
Glazer and Moynihan (1975, p. 1) remarked that “ethnicity seems to be a new term” — but the root is very old.

From the Greek ethnos, originally meaning “heathen” or “pagan”
Largely ignored by social science, with the notable exception of Max Weber



Two broad contemporary approaches: primordial and constructivist.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Primordialism
Ethnicity is a natural phenomenon, present throughout human history; modern ethnic groups have roots extending far into the past. Groups are defined by kinship and bloodlines.







Essentialist
The extreme version: ethnic groups are not merely historical but naturally occurring. Consistent with early-twentieth-century scientific racialism — the intellectual soil of eugenics and National Socialism (Smith 1999, pp. 4–7)


Historical
Ethnic groups are historical entities, extensions of kinship but more than kinship, defined by cultural signs — language, religion, traditions — that symbolize biological unity





Clifford Geertz (1973): ethnicity may not be a biological condition, but what matters is that humans perceive it as such — making it an objective condition, as real as if it were physical.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 108–109.
The Geertz move is subtle and students flatten it. He is not saying ethnicity is biologically real; he is saying the belief has real consequences, which is a sociological claim, not a genetic one. It is the hinge between the two approaches rather than a pure primordialist position.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Constructivism
Ethnicity and ethnic identity are malleable and flexible.

Weber: a “subjective belief” in “common descent. Whether or not an objective blood relationship exists” (1978, p. 389)
Schildkrout (1979, p. 184): the minimal definition is “the idea of common provenance, recruitment primarily through kinship, and a notion of distinctiveness, whether or not this consists of a unique inventory of cultural traits”
Benedict Anderson (1991): nations as imagined communities — socially constructed products of human interaction, maintained for instrumental reasons: to validate governance, to bind a community


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 109–110; Weber (1978, p. 389, cited in Guibernau and Rex 1997, p. 3); see also Horowitz (1985), Smith (1986), Schildkrout (1974).
Weber appears on both halves of this chapter — the Protestant ethic at the start and the subjective definition of ethnicity here. Worth pointing out: the same author is cited by the culturalists and by the constructivists.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: whose definition is this?
Max Weber defined ethnicity as a “subjective belief” in “common descent, whether or not an objective blood relationship exists.” This belongs to:

The primordial approach
The essentialist approach
The constructivist approach
The structural-functionalist approach



Constructivist. The clause that settles it is the second one: if the objective blood relationship is irrelevant, the identity is believed into being, not inherited.


[Key] Option 3. Options 1 and 2 are the two primordialist schools, and the pairing is deliberate — Weber appears on both halves of this chapter, cited by the culturalists for the Protestant ethic and by the constructivists here.
Any student who has him filed as “the traditional-authority man” will guess wrong, which is a useful lesson about reading authors rather than labels.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The modernist variant
A related claim: ethnicity is purely a modern invention, appearing only in the modern period of world history.

Marx and Engels — nations as a primarily bourgeois construct that would wither away after the collapse of capitalism
Hobsbawm (1990) — before the industrial era there was no ideal of politicized ethnic identities; these were created by modernization
Karl Deutsch (1953) — same point from the communications side



Note what this does to the causal story: if modernization creates politicized ethnicity, then ethnic conflict is not a survival from the past but a product of development.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 110; Deutsch (1953); Hobsbawm (1990).
Deutsch is the same author from Chapter 3 — social mobilization. Make the link: mobilization pulls people out of local worlds into national communication networks, and that is exactly when ethnic difference becomes politically legible. This is the strongest bridge in the chapter back to last week.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Nationalism as an ideology
Ethnicity can express itself politically in many ways. In the modern era many ethnic conflicts are couched as nationalist struggles — but, as Ishiyama and Breuning (1998) note, not all ethnopolitics is nationalistic.



Nationalism is a socio-political ideology whose core principles are:

Popular sovereignty — a people must have a state
The glorification of the community



Nationalists see the establishment and protection of the nation state as the highest political goal.




And if nationalism is an ideology like any other, there can be different types of it — some ethnic, some not.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: nationalism’s core principles
Ishiyama describes nationalism as a socio-political ideology with two core principles. They are:

Popular sovereignty — a people must have a state — and the glorification of the community
Self-determination and the equality of all citizens before the law
Ethnic purity and territorial expansion
The monopoly of legitimate force and the right to tax



Sovereignty and glorification. Nothing in either principle mentions ethnicity — which is exactly why there can be civic nationalisms as well as ethnic ones.


[Key] Option 1. Option 3 is the one to discuss: a student who equates nationalism with ethnic chauvinism has missed the move that makes Greenfeld’s typology possible in the first place.
Ishiyama is explicit, following Ishiyama and Breuning (1998), that not all ethnopolitics is nationalistic and not all nationalism is ethnic. Option 4 is Weber’s definition of the state, from Chapter 3 — a different thing entirely.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Greenfeld’s two dimensions
Greenfeld (1992) classifies nationalisms along two questions:


What is the nation? A collection of individuals (individualism), or a collective entity that is more than the sum of its parts (collectivism)?
Who belongs to the nation? Does citizenship alone qualify (civic), or is membership defined by blood (ethnic)?



These will importantly affect not only whether democracy emerges, but what form it takes if it does.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Table 4.3 · Types of nationalism

Ishiyama, Table 4.3








Civic
Ethnic




Individualism
Individualist / civic (US)
Not possible


Collectivism
Collectivist / civic (France)
Collectivist / ethnic (most of Eastern Europe)





Four cells, three logical types. One combination cannot exist — and working out why is the point of the table.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, Table 4.3, after Greenfeld (1992).
Do not give away the empty cell. Put the table up and ask the class why individualist/ethnic is impossible before you say anything. The next slide is the answer.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Reading Table 4.3

Individualist / civic — the US. The nation is a collection of individuals; membership rests (in theory) on allegiance to a set of principles enshrined in the Constitution. Individual rights are often held above the interests of the collective
Collectivist / civic — France. The nation is something more than a collection of individuals — La Belle France — yet who may belong is based on allegiance and, at least in principle, not on blood
Collectivist / ethnic — much of Central and Eastern Europe. The nation is a collective unit and membership is defined by blood and kinship



The third type is the most common and the most problematic for consolidating democracy: collective interests outrank individual rights, and blood descent gives outgroups no route into the national community. Under social and economic stress this breeds intolerance, incivility, and unwillingness to compromise with “outsiders.”


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 111–112; Greenfeld (1992).
The empty cell: defining the nation as a collection of individuals who are free to belong by allegiance is logically at odds with restricting membership by descent. Individualism makes membership a matter of the individual’s own commitment; ethnic membership makes it a matter of inheritance. The two criteria cannot both govern entry.
Caution students against reading the US cell as a description of American practice. Ishiyama writes “in theory” and means it; the gap between the civic self-description and the actual history of who counted is itself a comparative research question.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: why is one cell empty?
text:
Check: why is one cell empty?
Why does Greenfeld’s typology hold that individualist / ethnic nationalism is not possible?

No such country has yet been observed
Individualism makes belonging a matter of the individual’s own allegiance, which contradicts membership by inheritance
Ethnic nations are always large, and large nations are collectivist
Individualism and ethnicity are measured on the same dimension



Option 2. The exclusion is logical, not empirical — the two dimensions give contradictory answers to the question of how a person comes to belong.


[Key] Option 2. Option 1 is the trap, and a revealing one: students treat an empty cell in a typology as a gap in the data. It is worth stating the general rule — a typology’s empty cells are claims about what can be, and they are refuted by argument, not by searching harder for a case.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: Does diversity endanger democracy?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The pessimistic tradition







J. S. Mill (1958, p. 230)
“Free institutions are next to impossible in a country made up of different nationalities” — multinational societies as a continuous threat to social peace


Almond (1956)
The probability of violent conflict rises as a function of ethnic heterogeneity


Powell (1982)
A negative relationship between ethnic fractionalization and governmental stability, civil peace, and the prospects for democracy


Rabushka & Shepsle (1972)
Ethnic divisions are inimical to democracy — and democratic competition exacerbates ethnic conflict through ethnic outbidding by ethnic elites and their organizations


Reilly (2003)
Ethnic parties appeal specifically on ethnicity, so their emergence has a centrifugal effect — especially harmful where democratic institutions are fragile





The mechanism in the outbidding model: competing for the ethnic vote means mobilizing the group, and the cheapest way to mobilize is inflammatory “us versus them” rhetoric.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 112–114.
Even the pessimists mostly stop short of impossibility. David Welch’s formulation is the fair statement of the position: “establishing and sustaining democratic institutions in ethnically divided societies is a difficult task” (1993, p. 55).
Horowitz’s observation is the one students remember: “Democracy has progressed furthest in those East European countries that have the fewest serious ethnic cleavages (Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Poland) and progressed more slowly or not at all in those that are deeply divided (Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, and of course the former Yugoslavia)” (1993, p. 19).
Ask what is wrong with that as evidence. It is a correlation across a handful of cases with no control for the economic and institutional differences that also distinguish them — which is Lijphart’s many-variables, few-cases problem in the wild.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The revisionists







Fearon & Laitin (1996)
Ethnic heterogeneity does not predispose societies to conflict, civil war, or democratic collapse. Population size and the proportion of mountainous terrain matter far more to civil conflict than fractionalization


Horowitz (1985, 1993)
Conflict follows from diversity only at very high or very low fractionalization. Risk is highest where a majority group faces a very sizeable minority — Sinhalese and Tamils in Sri Lanka; Fijians and ethnic Indians in Fiji


Collier & Hoeffler (1998)
“Highly fractionalized societies are no more prone to war than highly homogeneous ones. The danger of civil war arises when the society is polarized into two groups”


Montalvo & Reynal-Querol (2005)
Polarization, not fractionalization, explains conflict


Reilly (2000)
In Papua New Guinea, so many groups that no one group could monopolize power — diversity promoted tolerance and coalition politics


Hardgrave (1993)
A similar argument for peace and democracy in India




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 114–115.
Fearon and Laitin’s mountains result is worth dwelling on for a minute, because it is a lesson in research design rather than a fact about mountains: a variable that correlates with conflict can be displaced entirely once a plausible rival is measured properly.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Fractionalization is not polarization

Fractionalization — how many groups there are, and how evenly the population divides among them.
Polarization — how far the distribution approaches two groups of comparable size facing one another.



Many small groups: high fractionalization, low polarization — and no group can rule alone
One majority against one sizeable minority: moderate fractionalization, high polarization — and the worst risk




This is why the early literature kept finding a relationship and the later literature kept failing to: they were measuring different things.


Connect to Chapter 7 and Session 7’s reading on electoral systems. Whether a cleavage structure becomes two blocs or many is partly an institutional choice, not only a demographic fact.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: fractionalization or polarization?
Collier and Hoeffler (1998) and Montalvo and Reynal-Querol (2005) conclude that civil conflict is best predicted by:

The number of ethnic groups
The degree of polarization into two opposed groups
The size of the largest ethnic group
The ratio of ethnic to religious cleavages



Polarization. Highly fractionalized societies are no more prone to war than highly homogeneous ones — the danger comes from a two-bloc structure, which is why Reilly’s Papua New Guinea, with very many groups, looks peaceful rather than explosive.


[Key] Option 2. Option 1 is the whole early literature’s answer, which is what makes it a good distractor — students who learned the pessimistic tradition first will pick it.
The payoff question: Horowitz’s “very high or very low fractionalization” claim and the polarization claim are close to the same claim stated in different vocabulary. Ask whether they are, and what data would distinguish them.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: It depends on institutions and elites
text:
It depends on institutions and elites
The recent literature treats ethnic cleavages as cost-effective strategic resources for group formation, interest definition and collective action (Fearon and Laitin 2003; Birnir 2007; Chandra 2004; Posner 2004), and makes the effect conditional.







Consociationalists
Represent groups broadly and you integrate subcultures into the political game. Securing minority representation integrates disaffected groups, which moderates their demands (Lorwin 1971; Nordlinger 1972; Daalder 1974; McRae 1974; Lijphart 1977)


Cohen (1997, p. 613)
“By making institutions more accessible and making ethnic cleavages more explicit, ethnic groups will engage in more frequent but less intense conflict”


Chandra (2004, 2005)
Attacks outbidding directly: institutions that restrict ethnic politics “to a single dimension destabilize democracy, whereas institutions that foster multiple dimensions of ethnic identity can sustain it” (2005, p. 236)


Birnir (2007)
Ethnic identity is a stable but flexible information shortcut; ethnic parties as “attractors” prefer peaceful routes to power. Violence follows from denial of access to the executive, not from the ethnification of politics




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 115–117.
Birnir’s logic is worth spelling out because it is a clean piece of reasoning: like all parties, ethnic parties seek leverage for a constituency; voters who use ethnic identity as a shortcut prefer parties that act for that constituency; so the attractor has a strong incentive to reach the executive, and the peaceful route is the reliable one. The deviation to be explained is therefore not peace but exclusion.
Her question is the good exam question: why do members of some ethnic groups peacefully support their group in electoral politics while others exit and turn to protest and violence? Her answer is access.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: what produces the violence?
Birnir finds the ethnification of politics does not by itself produce violence. When violence does occur, it results from:

The sheer number of ethnic groups competing in a system
The presence of ethnic parties, which inevitably escalate demands through outbidding
The denial of political access — particularly restrictions on access to the executive
The collapse of traditional authority structures during modernization



Exclusion from power. The deviation to be explained is not peace but shutting out — ethnic parties prefer the peaceful route because it is the reliable one.


[Key] Option 3. Option 2 is Rabushka and Shepsle’s outbidding — a correct statement of a different position, and the position Chandra and Birnir are both writing against, which makes it the strongest wrong answer. Option 1 is closer to Horowitz and the fractionalization literature.
Pair this with the Elkins and Simeon rule from Part 2. Both say the same thing in different vocabulary: when a cultural or ethnic explanation looks compelling, check whether an institutional one — who is shut out of power — explains it better first.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Where this leaves the argument

Ishiyama’s own summing up: there is little question that culture and ethnopolitics have some kind of effect — while the debate over whether culture is independent, and whether diversity kills democracy, remains open.


Two conclusions he does commit to:

Where political cultures value tolerance, moderation, compromise and civility, democracy is easier to develop
Deeply divided societies face greater challenges, but democracy is not impossible there




What is decisive is how democratic institutions are designed, and whether they fit a particular ethnic and cultural context — as in a place as divided as Iraq.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s article: Posner (2004)
Posner, “The Political Salience of Cultural Difference” — cited in this chapter among the contingent accounts, and the reason it belongs beside it.

The Chewa and Tumbuka straddle the Zambia–Malawi border: the same cultural difference, the same colonial-era history
In Malawi they are political adversaries; in Zambia they are allies
The difference is not the cleavage but the political arena: group size relative to the national electorate determines whether the difference is a useful coalitional building block



Read it as a design as much as an argument — a natural experiment that holds culture constant and varies the arena, which is how you test whether identity is politically salient rather than merely present.


Posner is the Session 5 article. Two reasons to spend time on it.
First, substance: it is the sharpest available answer to this chapter’s central question — identities become political when political entrepreneurs find them useful at the scale at which they must build a coalition. That is the constructivist and institutionalist answer rolled together.
Second, method: it is a most-similar-systems design of the kind Lijphart recommended in Session 1, and students should be able to name it as such without prompting by now. Ask what is held constant, what varies, and what the inference rests on.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Can outsiders promote democracy — and how much of a country’s regime was ever decided inside its borders at all?


Every chapter so far has explained democracy from the inside: history, economics, culture, and next time social structure. Chapter 6 turns the camera around.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 6, pp. 134–156.
The one exception Ishiyama names is dependency theory from Chapter 3, which was already an external account. Everything else — Moore’s historical sequences, Lipset’s modernization, Almond and Verba’s culture — has treated the country as the container of its own explanation.
Four external forces in this chapter: diffusion and waves, colonial legacy, globalization, and imposition. Keep them distinct; students blur the last three into “foreign influence.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class you should be able to:

Describe Huntington’s three waves and two reverse waves, and say what definition of democracy he is counting
Name the causes of the third wave, and explain why a global recession produces democratization
Distinguish transformation, replacement and transplacement, and say which Huntington prefers
Place an authoritarian regime on Bratton and Van de Walle’s two dimensions and predict its transition
State the clash of civilizations thesis and two serious objections to it
Contrast indirect and direct colonial rule, and name a cost of each
Explain why globalization might produce conflict rather than dissolve it
List Enterline and Greig’s four conditions for an imposed democracy to survive

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: Waves of democratization

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Huntington’s metaphor

Throw a stone into a pond. Democratization arrives in concentric waves spreading outward — each followed by a reverse wave of contraction.


The waves were driven in part by war and the spread of democratic ideals — ideals “often carried at the barrel of a gun,” whether by Napoleon’s armies or by the occupation forces of the United States and the West.



Before you accept the count, ask what is being counted. For Huntington, democracy means the conduct of competitive elections — Schumpeter’s minimalist definition from Chapter 1, not consolidated democracy.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 134–136; Huntington, The Third Wave (1991).
Push the definitional point hard, because every number on the next slide depends on it. A “wave” of electoral democracies is a different claim from a wave of liberal consolidated ones, and the gap between those two is exactly what the hybrid-regimes literature later exploits.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three waves, two reverses

Built from Ishiyama ch. 6; counts are Huntington’s








Wave
Period
Trigger
Count




First wave
1820s → end of WWI
Ideals of the French Revolution of 1789; liberty, equality, brotherhood
29 democracies by the end of WWI


First reverse
1920s–1930s
Fascism in Italy, then Germany; coups installing military and royal dictatorships across central and eastern Europe
down to 12


Second wave
1945 → 1962
The end of the formal global empires; rapid decolonization in Asia and Africa
36 countries by 1962


Second reverse
1960–1975
Persistent poverty, political instability, and the machinations of both superpowers during the Cold War
sharply reduced


Third wave
from 1974–75
Portugal, Spain, Greece → Latin America → East Asia → the post-communist world → Africa
ongoing, and contested




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 135–137.
The first wave’s long tail matters: the ideal of self-determination of peoples fed the nationalist tensions that undermined the Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian Empires and helped precipitate World War I. A democratizing wave with a world war as a downstream consequence is a useful corrective to any simple story of progress.
The third wave’s opening is three deaths and a defeat in one year: Portugal’s military dictatorship collapses, Franco dies, and the Greek junta falls after the Greco-Turkish conflict over Cyprus in 1974.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What caused the third wave?







The oil shock
Economic boom through the 1950s and 1960s, then the OPEC boycott after the 1973 Yom Kippur War and a major global slowdown


Performance legitimacy collapses
Many authoritarian regimes had bought loyalty with growth — jobs, education, welfare. No growth, no legitimacy (Bergesen 1992)


A new middle class
The boom produced social mobilization and a much larger middle class; the downturn hit it hardest, and it led the demands in Spain and Portugal (Bermeo 1987)


Vatican II
Reforms under Pope Paul II, 1963–65, turned national Catholic churches from defenders of the status quo into opponents of authoritarianism


The West withdraws its cover
After Vietnam and under Carter’s human-rights emphasis, the US and the European Community stopped unconditionally backing anti-communist dictatorships


The snowball
Each democratization supplied a model for emulation — a regional diffusion effect (Shin 1994; Starr 1991; Modelski and Perry 1991)




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 137–139.
Performance legitimacy is the hinge, and it is the same concept from Chapter 4’s subject political culture. Say so: a regime that rests its claim on outputs has written itself a contract it cannot always honour, and a global recession is an exogenous shock that calls it in.
On diffusion, Starr’s own finding is more careful than the headline: emulation operated at a regional level for some of the world system, not all. Note the cultural and linguistic channel — Portugal and Spain democratizing first, then Latin America, is not a coincidence of geography.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: why would a recession produce democratization?
text:
Note: why would a recession produce democratization?
In Ishiyama’s account of the third wave, a global economic downturn pushes authoritarian regimes toward democratization because:

International lenders made democratic reform a condition of credit
Poorer countries can no longer afford a repressive apparatus
Regimes that based their legitimacy on economic performance could no longer deliver it, weakening their claim in the eyes of citizens
Recessions reduce inequality, and lower inequality favours democracy



Performance legitimacy fails. A regime that bought loyalty with growth has nothing to offer when growth stops — and the grievance is aimed directly at the regime.


[Key] Option 3. Option 2 is plausible-sounding and wrong in this chapter — repression is usually cheap; it is co-optation that is expensive.
Bergesen’s addition is worth a sentence: developing states are more constrained than core states in how they can respond to a global recession, so the same shock has a bigger political effect at the periphery.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Four sub-waves, four degrees of difficulty
text:
Four sub-waves, four degrees of difficulty

Built from Ishiyama ch. 6









Sub-wave
Cases
Economy
Prior democracy
Other conditions




First
Greece, Portugal, Spain
Developed capitalist market economies
Yes — experiments in the 1920s–30s
Close to democratic Europe; few deep cleavages (Spain aside)


Second
Latin America
Less developed, but basically market economies
Yes, for the most part
Significantly more culturally diverse; transitions drawn out


Third
The former communist world
Centrally planned — a triple transition
Little or none
New national identity to build; little civil society after totalitarianism


Fourth
Africa and the Middle East
Often resource-dependent
Rarely
Lacking the posited preconditions, and “cursed” with resources





The “triple transition”: out of communist authoritarianism, out of central planning, and into a national identity the old ideology had denied.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 139–141.
This table is the chapter’s best single teaching device, because it converts “the third wave” from one event into four with different odds. Ask students which row their focal country sits closest to, even if it is not literally in that region.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The resource curse
Hazem Beblawi (1987): states rich in oil become rentier states — they generate revenue by selling high-value commodities abroad rather than by taxing citizens.








No taxes, no leverage
Citizens have less incentive to press the government to be responsive


No taxes, no obligation
The state has less incentive to respond, since revenue comes from external rents, not from them


Bribes, not participation
Where the state does respond, it buys the population off with welfare and material allocation rather than broadening participation (Feldman 2003)


Bloated bureaucracy, corruption
State control of resource access makes office a route to wealth (Quinn 2002)




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 141–142.
The mechanism is the thing to carry away, and it runs backwards through Tilly from the Chapter 3 lecture: no extraction, no bargaining, no rights. Taxation is not merely how states get money — it is what forces them into a relationship with citizens. Oil severs it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: How transitions happen

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four actors, two camps
Transitions are shaped by who holds power inside each camp.







Hardliners (regime)
Want to cling to power


Softliners (regime)
Willing to negotiate, particularly to preserve their authority as circumstances change


Radicals (opposition)
Want the immediate replacement of the regime


Moderates (opposition)
Willing to negotiate to keep the transfer of power peaceful





The transition process has an independent effect on whether democracy survives — context correlates with democracy, but the process itself does work of its own (O’Donnell, Schmitter and Whitehead 1986; Przeworski 1986, 1991).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Huntington’s three transitions

Built from Ishiyama ch. 6, after Huntington (1991)







Type
Who leads
Huntington’s words




Transformation
The regime — mostly reformers within it
“The elites in power [take] the lead in bringing about democracy” (1991, p. 153)


Replacement
The opposition
“Opposition [takes] the lead … and the authoritarian regime collapses or is overthrown” (p. 154)


Transplacement
Both, by negotiation
“Democratization results largely from joint action by government and opposition group” (p. 156)





Transplacement happens when neither side is strong enough to dominate. It succeeds only if the reformers control their hardliners and the moderates control their radicals — two internal fights before the external one.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: which transition does Huntington prefer?
text:
Note: which transition does Huntington prefer?
Huntington argues the preferable routes to democracy are:

Transplacement only, since negotiated settlements are the only durable kind
Whichever route is fastest, since prolonged transitions invite reversal
Replacement, because a clean break removes the old elite
Transformation or transplacement, because replacement brings confrontation, violence and rapid turnover



Transformation or transplacement — and not replacement. “Stable democracies and near-democracies are likely to result from rather slow evolutionary process than from revolutionary overthrow of existing hegemonies” (Huntington 1984, p. 41).


[Key] Option 4. Option 3 is the intuition most students arrive with, and it is worth naming why it fails here: replacements are often characterized by rapid turnover, political instability, and a new “democratic” regime willing to use force to secure its own authority.
Option 1 is the near-miss — transplacement is preferred, but so is transformation, and an item that forces students to notice “and not” is testing whether they read the sentence or the heading.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Kitschelt: two kinds of communism
Herbert Kitschelt (1994) on why post-communist transitions diverged.









Patrimonial communism
National consensus communism




Rule
Personalist; hierarchical chains of personal dependence between leaders and followers
Contestation and interest articulation permitted


Elite contestation
Low
Some


Bureaucracy
Little rational-legal professionalization
A degree of professionalization


Dissent
Barely tolerated; democratic centralism emphasized
Tolerated in exchange for compliance with the system’s basics


Examples
—
Hungary, Poland



: Built from Ishiyama ch. 6, after Kitschelt (1994) {tbl-colwidths=“[22,39,39]”}


Transitions from national consensus communism are likeliest to succeed: enough internal competition had been permitted that the relevant actors were willing to compromise and negotiate — that is, to transplace.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 144–145.
Poland and Hungary also appealed to a degree of nationalism and charted an economic course somewhat independent of Moscow, which gave regimes originally imposed by the Soviet Union a measure of homegrown legitimacy.
The general claim is the transferable one: the previous regime structures the transition, and the transition structures the politics that follow. That is a three-link causal chain and students should be able to recite it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Bratton and Van de Walle: Africa’s four types
text:
Bratton and Van de Walle: Africa’s four types
Neo-patrimonial regimes — authority derived not from ideology or institution but from personal connection to “the big man,” through networks of patron–client relations.

Built from Ishiyama ch. 6, after Bratton and Van de Walle (1994, 1997)








Mass participation low
Mass participation encouraged




Elite competition low
Personalist dictatorship — Zaire under Mobutu
Plebiscitary one-party — Zambia under Kaunda


Elite competition higher
Military oligarchy — Nigeria for most of its independence
Competitive one-party — Tanzania under Nyerere





A fifth type sits outside the grid: the settler regimes — South Africa, Rhodesia — in reality much more like European-dominated colonial regimes, and leaving a very different legacy.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 145–147.
Two dimensions, same logic as Huntington’s Table 3.2 from the Chapter 3 lecture: elite competition and mass participation. Worth saying explicitly that this is the second 2×2 of the course built on “how much competition, how much participation” — it is a recurring way of carving up authoritarianism.
Note that participation in a plebiscitary system is officially mobilized, usually to stage mass shows of support. Participation is not the same as influence.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Note: which regime transitions worst?
On Bratton and Van de Walle’s account, the most difficult transitions occur in countries whose previous regime was a:

Personalist dictatorship
Competitive one-party system
Military oligarchy
Plebiscitary one-party system



Personalist dictatorship. The dictator’s personal survival is tied to the regime’s, so any reform reads as a direct personal threat — and he is unlikely to countenance change, let alone step down, absent a guarantee of his own safety.


[Key] Option 1. Option 2 is the mirror-image trap: competitive one-party systems transition best, for the same reason Kitschelt gives for national consensus communism — some internal competition had already taught elites to bargain.
The mechanism is worth stating as a general rule: the more a regime is identical with one person, the fewer exits that person has, and the fewer exits, the more violent the ending.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: A reverse wave?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The clash of civilizations
Huntington’s cultural argument is not Chapter 4’s political culture. Here culture means civilizational world views, indicated by dominant religion.








Zone
What defines it
Implication for democracy




Western Christian
Individual liberties; separation of Church and State; the right to rule derived from the consent of the governed
Most conducive


Orthodox Christian
Fusion of State and Church from the Byzantine inheritance; Moscow as the “Third Rome”; authority from divine right — continued by communist rule claiming the laws of history
Less conducive


Confucian
Less a religion than a social ideology of hierarchy, family-like structures, collective interests over individual rights against the state
Not conducive — though Korea and Taiwan suggest the impediment is weaker than Huntington thought


Islamic
Egalitarianism and popular participation support democracy; the absence of separation between secular and religious authority undermines it
Contains elements both congenial and uncongenial




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 147–150.
Do not let the Islamic row pass as a simple negative. Ishiyama is careful: Huntington names egalitarianism and popular participation in the political community as supportive, and theocracy as the impediment, because a ruler executing the will of God does not need the consent of the governed.
Japan and the Philippines are Huntington’s awkward cases, explained away by weak Confucian penetration — the Philippines under Portuguese, Spanish and American control, and Japan where Confucianism arrived late and reached mainly the upper classes. An explanation that has to explain away its exceptions is worth flagging as such.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four objections

Overly simplistic — it ignores significant differences between countries inside one civilization
Arbitrary taxonomy — the classification is especially unconvincing along the borders of civilizations
Wrong causes — it neglects ideological mobilization and unfulfilled socioeconomic needs, the real drivers of conflict, reducing everything to cultural determinism
Self-fulfilling — the more people believe conflict is culturally determined, the more likely it becomes



Objection 4 is the unusual one, and worth holding onto: a theory of politics can help bring about the world it describes.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, p. 150; see Rubinstein and Crocker (1994) for the fuller list.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Did the wave produce democracies — or hybrids?
text:
Did the wave produce democracies — or hybrids?
Carothers (2002); Diamond (2002); Levitsky and Way (2002); Ottaway (2003): the transitions of the 1990s mostly produced hybrid systems — not fully democratic, not fully authoritarian.

In Africa and Latin America, human rights violations and military interference were widespread enough that observers hesitated to call these regimes democratic
After the Soviet break-up, regimes holding free and fair elections while retaining authoritarian traits kept multiplying



Most scholars at first treated these as transitional — the “transition paradigm.” That assumption started to break down in the mid-1990s: a growing number of scholars suspected hybrid regimes were not transitional but remarkably stable.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 150–151; Carothers (2002); Levitsky and Way (2002); Ottaway (2003).
This is the bridge to today’s article, and the single most important idea in the chapter for their dossiers. The transition paradigm assumed a destination. If hybrid regimes are a stable type rather than a waypoint, then “how far along is this country?” is the wrong question, and “what kind of regime is this, and what sustains it?” is the right one.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: what is the transition paradigm?
text:
Note: what is the transition paradigm?
The “transition paradigm” that Carothers and others came to question was the assumption that:

Democratization always proceeds in waves
Regimes that hold elections while retaining authoritarian traits are temporary and will become full democracies
Every country will eventually democratize if given enough time
Foreign assistance is necessary for any transition to succeed



That hybrids are a waypoint. The suspicion that broke it: these regimes were not transitional but displayed remarkable stability — a destination, not a stage.


[Key] Option 2. Option 3 is the looser folk version of the same idea and will attract students who have the gist but not the claim; the paradigm was specifically about how to classify regimes that had already changed, not a general optimism about history.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: The legacy of colonialism

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Does colonial heritage matter at all?
text:
Does colonial heritage matter at all?







The Eurocentric view
Democracy spread as European values and traditions spread; the colonizer transmitted culture, language, and institutions conducive to democracy (Weiner 1989)


No relationship
Barro (1999); Quainoo (2000)


British colonies specifically
Being a former British colony raises the probability of democracy (Lipset et al. 1993; Clague et al. 2001)





Weiner’s (1989) observation. By 1983, every Third World country that emerged from colonial rule after WWII with a population of at least one million — and almost all the smaller ones — and a continuous democratic experience was a former British colony.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 151–152.
Worth a methodological minute. Weiner’s observation is striking and is also a selection problem waiting to be named: Britain colonized particular kinds of places, and the colonies it granted independence to first were the ones it judged ready. The finding is real; its causal reading is not automatic.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Indirect and direct rule
Khapoya (1998) distinguishes two colonial styles in Africa.

Built from Ishiyama ch. 6, after Khapoya (1998)








Indirect rule (British)
Direct rule (French, Portuguese, Belgian)




Aim
Not assimilation — share skills, values and culture to let Africans run their own communities; society segregated between natives and whites
The colony as an extension of the mother country; in Algeria, active assimilation


Method
Co-opt the local power structure — kings, chiefs, headmen — by invitation, coercion or bribery
All commands flow from the metropole, enforced by regional governors


Local elites
Expected to enforce laws, collect taxes, buffer between natives and colonial authority
Staffed the colonial state, but trained to implement policy, not make it


Benefit
Real experience of self-rule; mimicked British electoral, legislative and judicial institutions
An anti-colonial cooperative ethos across ethnic lines, directed at a common enemy


Cost
Reinforced ethnic and tribal division — some groups arbitrarily privileged over others
Local elites poorly equipped for self-rule at independence




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 152–154.
The symmetry is the point and it is genuinely elegant: each style of rule bought one thing at the price of the other. Indirect rule bought governing experience and paid in ethnic division; direct rule bought cross-ethnic solidarity and paid in inexperience.
Britain’s greater willingness to grant independence after WWII follows from the same logic — the colonies looked ready because they had been run that way — while France, Belgium and Portugal resisted decolonization and kept pressing assimilation.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: the cost of indirect rule
text:
Note: the cost of indirect rule
Indirect rule left British colonies better prepared for self-government. Its principal cost, in Ishiyama’s account, was that it:

Reinforced ethnic and tribal division by arbitrarily privileging some groups over others
Prevented the growth of a native bureaucratic elite
Delayed independence relative to French and Belgian colonies
Left colonies economically dependent on Britain after independence



Ethnic division. Weiner and Huntington’s term for where it leads is the ethnic hegemonic state — one in which “a single ethnic group has taken control over the state and used its powers to exercise control over others” (1987, p. 35).


[Key] Option 1. Options 2 and 3 are both the opposite of the record — indirect rule produced native administrative experience, and Britain decolonized earlier, not later.
Connect forward: an ethnic hegemonic state is a Chapter 4 problem arriving through a Chapter 6 mechanism. The cleavage is colonial in origin and ethnic in expression.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: Globalization

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: What globalization is, and the optimistic case
text:
What globalization is, and the optimistic case

Globalization: increasing economic interdependence among the countries of the world, creating a multiplicity of linkages, interconnections and interdependence — a process by which “events, decisions, and activities in one part of the world can come to have significant consequences for individuals and communities in quite distant parts of the globe” (McGrew and Lewis 1995, p. 23).


Baker, Epstein and Pollin (1998) identify three consequences: more international economic interaction; qualitative change in how states operate within an economy; and less power for states, more for private business and market forces.



The optimistic case is short and familiar: globalization stimulates market growth and development, development generates wealth, and wealth is positively related to democracy — which is Chapter 3’s argument, imported.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The pessimistic case
The “chaos” or “primordialist” perspective (Sadowski): conflict rises as a backlash against globalization’s encroachments on identity.







Homogenization provokes
A universalizing set of Western values elicits reactions that exalt difference and local particularism — resistance “rooted in an imagined past that never was”


Media erodes
Television and the internet erode traditional values and moral restraints


Movement competes
Falling transport costs move goods and people; competition for jobs plus frustrated aspirations breeds resentment and scapegoating


Kotkin (1993)
Globalization breeds a new wave of ethnic awareness — prosperity for some, for others “a throwback to the basest kind of clannishness”


Naisbitt (1994)
A new “tribalism”; telecommunications let ethnic groups coordinate and go it alone, so separatism grows and conflict follows


Chua (2002)
Market-dominant minorities control disproportionate wealth; globalization makes them richer while the poorer majority gains little — a catalyst for strife along lines that already existed




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 155–157.
Chua is the most useful for dossiers because her mechanism is specific and checkable: look for a minority that is both economically dominant and ethnically marked, then ask what happened to the gap during liberalization.
Wright and Macmanus (1991) supply the irony worth quoting: the hope was that economic interdependence would bring “world harmony,” and the new intimacy of trade and financial flows instead provoked the political and cultural backlashes that seeded conflict.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Globalization inside the rich democracies
A separate literature asks what globalization does to democracies that already exist. Its answer: it undermines the Left.

Owners of mobile capital can relocate abroad; domestic producers face foreign competition
More dynamic, competitive and interdependent markets undermine older forms of production, pushing toward smaller production units (Turner 1991)
Decentralized, capital-intensive production means less labour solidarity and weaker organized labour — and so weaker left parties



Social democratic and socialist parties became more economically conservative — on workplace regulation, redistributive taxation, and the welfare state (Piazza 2001).




Kitschelt’s twist: parties with loose internal structures and weaker union ties adapted; “entrenched” parties with strong labour ties could not manoeuvre, and lost ground.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Note: what is a market-dominant minority?
text:
Note: what is a market-dominant minority?
Amy Chua argues globalization is a catalyst for ethnic strife where there is a market-dominant minority — that is:

The foreign investors who come to dominate a liberalizing economy
A minority that migrated for economic reasons and remains unassimilated
An ethnic minority that holds political office disproportionately
An ethnic minority controlling a disproportionate share of the country’s wealth, which globalization enriches further while the poorer majority gains little



Disproportionate wealth, not office. And note Chua’s careful limit: globalization ignites the conflict, but the lines of conflict already existed.


[Key] Option 4. Option 3 swaps economic dominance for political dominance, which is nearer to Chapter 4’s ethnic hegemonic state — a good distractor precisely because both concepts are in this course.
The qualifier in the callout is the part students drop. Chua is not claiming globalization creates ethnic division; she is claiming it loads an existing division with new economic resentment.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 6: Imposed democracy

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Democracy installed from outside

Imposed democracy: “democratic governments installed by a foreign power in which the foreign power plays an important role in the establishment, promotion, and maintenance of the institutions of government” (Enterline and Greig 2008).


Not new. The Netherlands in the seventeenth century, the United Kingdom in the eighteenth and nineteenth, the United States in the twentieth — each promoted a global ideology and sought to reshape countries in its mould.


Three routes:

After defeat in war — occupation, removal of the government, entirely new institutions: West Germany and Japan; more recently Iraq and Afghanistan
Through the colonial process — the colonial power sets up the regime that governs after independence
Covertly — including support for a coup d’état




What they share: the means of governance are established through the actions and decisions of a foreign power.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Four conditions — and why they rarely hold
text:
Four conditions — and why they rarely hold
Gills et al. (1993): at best, external intervention produces only nominal “low-intensity democracies.”

Enterline and Greig (2008) are more conditional. Imposed democracies can survive given:

A large occupation force
A clear message of sustained, long-term occupation behind the new state
An ethnically homogeneous society
Democratic neighbours




Now read that list against the third and fourth sub-waves — Iraq, Afghanistan. These conditions do not hold in most of the countries where imposition has been tried, so the prospects are not good.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 6, pp. 158–159.
Ask the class to score a case against the four criteria out loud. West Germany and Japan pass all four or nearly; Iraq passes at most one. That exercise does more than the list.
Note also that conditions 3 and 4 are not things an occupier can supply. Two of the four preconditions for success are entirely outside the intervener’s control, which is a serious finding about the limits of policy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Where this leaves the argument

Ishiyama’s summing up: external forces do not determine whether democracy emerges — but diffusion, globalization and imposition cannot be discounted.


Taken together with history, culture, economics and social structure, these external forces powerfully shape what happens inside a country.



But the chapter ends by pointing somewhere else: whether a country ultimately develops along democratic lines depends powerfully on the institutional choices made at the inception of the democratic experiment. That is Chapter 7, and the rest of the course.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s article: Levitsky and Way
“Linkage versus Leverage” — the natural companion, since Levitsky and Way are among the scholars this chapter credits with naming hybrid regimes.







Leverage
A government’s vulnerability to external democratizing pressure — sanctions, conditionality, diplomatic punishment


Linkage
The density of a country’s ties to the democratic West — economic, political, social, organizational, communication





Their claim is that linkage does more work than leverage. Pressure applied to a weak state can force an election; dense ties change what domestic actors want and what they can get away with.


Two reasons to spend time on it.
First, it sharpens this whole chapter. “External influence” is not one variable: a coercive channel and a connective channel behave differently, and the chapter’s diffusion, colonial and globalization stories are mostly linkage stories.
Second, for dossiers: leverage is what a policy memo usually proposes, and linkage is what usually explains the outcome. A team recommending external pressure should say which of the two it is relying on.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
For your dossier
Round 3 — the causal argument and the rival you rejected — was due this session. Chapter 6 supplies the rival most teams forget to consider.
Four things to try this week:

Ask whether your focal country’s regime change was a transformation, replacement, or transplacement, and what that predicts about the politics that followed
Place its previous regime on Bratton and Van de Walle’s two dimensions, or Kitschelt’s pair, and check the prediction against the record
If it is resource-rich, test the rentier mechanism directly: what share of revenue comes from taxation?
If your argument is entirely domestic, name the external explanation you are rejecting and say why. “I did not think about it” is not a rejection

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Why do some six-minute presentations persuade a room, while others with better research do not?


Halfway through the semester, the problem is rarely the research. It is design (what goes in the six minutes), teamwork (who carries which part), and exchange (what happens in the four minutes after).

Sources - Karl Ho, “How to give a killer presentation” (Math and Coding Camp deck), slides.com/karlho/mcc_howtogiveakillerpresentation - BARBRI, “5 presentation skills every lawyer needs,” barbri.com/resources/5-presentation-skills-every-lawyer-needs - Karl Ho, “How to discuss/review,” slides.com/karlho/how-to-discuss-review - PSCI 3350 presentation rubric (rubrics/presentation_rubric.qmd)
Timing: we are between Rounds 3 and 4. Teams have presented two or three times, so the advice will land on experience rather than on theory. Ask the room before starting: “Which team ran over time at least once?” Usually most hands go up.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class you should be able to:

Explain why oral advocacy is a core skill for law school and the profession
Build a six-minute presentation around one contestable sentence
Divide preparation and delivery evenly across a team of three to five
Design slides that anchor speech instead of replacing it
Answer a question the way an advocate answers a judge
Discuss another team’s presentation as a constructive pre-reviewer

section: Part 1: Why this matters for future lawyers
text: Part 1: Why this matters for future lawyers

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Law begins in story

“The law always begins in story.” — James Boyd White


A brief persuades a reader; oral argument persuades a listener who can interrupt you
The 1L Socratic method is a cold call with follow-ups. You have been practicing it since September
Moot court, client meetings, firm interviews and hearings all use the same skill: a clear claim, under time pressure, defended under questioning


Public speaking is the one skill machines do not replace. You can have a model draft your outline. You cannot have it stand at the podium and answer a judge.

Sources BARBRI (White quotation); Ho, Math and Coding Camp deck, opening slide (citing Carmine Gallo in Inc.: public speaking as the irreplaceable skill).
Point out the connection to our course design: the December 3 hearing is structured like an oral argument, with stakeholders questioning the team. Every round before it is practice for that hearing.
Link to the AI policy: Criterion E (response to questions) is where oral verification happens. That only works because a person has to answer live.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Part 2: Design — six minutes, one argument
text: Part 2: Design — six minutes, one argument

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Start from one sentence
Before any slide exists, the team writes one contestable sentence: the claim a reasonable classmate could disagree with.



A topic
“Kenya’s electoral system and ethnic politics.”

A claim
“Kenya’s 2010 county system reduced the stakes of the presidency less than Ghana’s party system did, because …”



If the team cannot agree on the sentence, it is not ready to make slides.

Sources Ho, Math and Coding Camp deck (“state your research question at the beginning”); rubric Criterion A (“the argument is stated as one contestable sentence and defended”).
The Kenya/Ghana claim is deliberately incomplete; finish it with the room. The point is the form: comparative, causal, and arguable.
Legal analogue: a question presented in a brief. A judge who cannot restate your question after thirty seconds will not follow the rest.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Structure: tell them three times
Aristotle’s rule, as BARBRI puts it: tell them what you are going to tell them, tell them, then tell them what you told them.








Segment
Time
Job




Open
0:40
The problem, the pairing, the claim


Body
4:30
Three supports: the round’s three requirements


Close
0:50
Claim restated, one implication, the open question




The rubric already asks for three things per round. Your body has three parts. That is not a coincidence.

Sources BARBRI, skill 2 (structuring arguments; grouping points in threes; Aristotle); Ho deck, on-stage items 2 and 8 (“state your question at the beginning”; “repeat the main takeaways at the end”); rubric “What each round is asking for.”
Transitions do the structural work aloud: “That is the context. Now the mechanism.” A listener cannot flip back a page.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Concede the weak point

Conceding a weaker point makes your stronger arguments more credible. — David Emanuel KC (via BARBRI)


Round 3 already requires it: the rival explanation you rejected
Rounds 4–5: the trade-off and the failure mode
A team that names its own limitation first takes the best question away from the audience


Sources BARBRI, skill 2; rubric Rounds 3–5.
This is the most law-school-specific advice in the lecture. Courts reward candor; opposing counsel will find the weakness anyway. Comparative-politics version: say which confounder your pairing does not control (Round 1, point ii).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The arithmetic of six minutes

Speaking pace ≈ 130 words a minute → about 780 words in total
18 auto-advancing slides × 20 seconds = 6:00 → about 43 words spoken per slide
A slide with 100 words of text cannot be read and listened to in 20 seconds


Cut until it hurts, then cut one more slide. What you cut goes to the appendix for questions.

Sources Sept 3 workshop, “six-minute arithmetic”; Ho deck, final slide (put technical detail such as code, extra charts and screenshots in an appendix after the talk for Q&A).
Effect = f(main takeaway, time, skills, audience) from the Math and Coding Camp deck: the six-minute limit decides what the takeaway can be, not the other way round.
If time allows, rerun the workshop demonstration: put a dense slide up for 20 seconds and ask a student to summarize it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Part 3: Slides that anchor, not replace
text: Part 3: Slides that anchor, not replace

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Making great (not good) slides

Figures first, then tables, then text. People process pictures faster than words
Legible fonts, never the default. Test from the back row of FO 3.616
One idea per slide, with a headline that states it
Every number carries year, source and caveat, as the dossier does
Fancy effects sparingly: use one only when the payoff exceeds what it costs the audience to learn it


Sources Ho deck, “Making great (not good) slides” items 1–4; BARBRI skill 3 (picture superiority effect; visuals complement delivery, do not replace it); rubric Criterion B.
“Headline that states it”: not “Election results” but “Kenya’s 2013 winner cleared 50% by less than one point.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Fix this slide


Before
Kenya 2013 Election. The 2013 presidential election in Kenya was held on March 4. Uhuru Kenyatta won with 50.07% of the vote according to the IEBC. The opposition challenged the result in the Supreme Court, which upheld it. This shows that Kenya’s institutions …

After
Kenya 2013: the win depended on the denominator

50.07% (rejected ballots counted) vs 50.51% (excluded)
Threshold: 50% + 1
Source: IEBC; Supreme Court petition 2013



The speaker supplies the sentence. The slide supplies the number the audience must remember.

Sources Kenya/Ghana dossier, “What we could not verify” appendix and the 50.07 vs 50.51 discussion.
Exercise (3 minutes, in teams): take one slide from your own Round 3 deck and apply the same edit. Collect one before/after from a volunteer team.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check the number before you cite it
text:
Check the number before you cite it
BARBRI repeats a famous claim: meaning is 7% words, 38% tone, 55% body language (Mehrabian).

Mehrabian’s experiments measured how listeners judged feelings from single words when tone and words conflicted
He has said himself that the ratios do not apply to ordinary communication
So: your words still carry the argument. Tone and posture decide whether the room trusts you


A cited number that does not say what you claim is the fastest way to lose a judge or a seminar.

Sources BARBRI, skill 4; Mehrabian, Silent Messages (1971), and Mehrabian’s own caveats on the scope of the 7-38-55 findings.
This slide does double duty: nonverbal delivery matters, and the course’s verification standard applies to presentation advice too. Same rule as the dossiers: every number carries its source and its scope.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Part 4: Teamwork — evenly prepared, evenly shared
text: Part 4: Teamwork — evenly prepared, evenly shared

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
One argument, not four segments
The rubric’s Criterion C rewards a presentation that sounds like one mind. That comes from how the work is divided, not from rehearsing the handoffs.

Divide by function, not by “you take slides 1–5”
Everyone can present every slide. The rotating speaker is a role, not the only person who understands the argument
Everyone is ready for questions. Non-speakers are visibly prepared to support


Sources Rubric Criterion C; syllabus (speaker rotates every round); Ho deck, “emphasize teamwork.”
The failure mode we have already seen in Rounds 1–3: four members each prepare a segment, meet the night before, and stitch. The result repeats itself, contradicts itself, and nobody can answer a question outside their segment.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: On stage

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Delivery

Look at the audience, not the screen. The slides advance on their own
State the claim in the first 40 seconds
Stand balanced, vary pace and volume; pause after the key number
Notes, not a script. Reading aloud loses Criterion D points
Never run over time. At 6:00 the clock stops, and anything after it earns nothing


Sources Ho deck, “On stage” items 1–4 and 9–10; BARBRI skill 4; rubric Criteria B and D.
Practical tip: put a clicker or phone timer on the lectern, but with auto-advance the slides are already your timer. If you fall behind, skip a sentence. Do not try to catch up by talking faster.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Answering questions like an advocate

Answer the question actually asked, in the first sentence: yes, no, or “it depends on …”
Give the reason, then the evidence
If you do not know: say so, and say what would settle it
Concede and pivot when the questioner is right
Route to a teammate by plan, not by panic: “Our evidence lead checked that figure. Maria?”


Sources Rubric Criterion E; BARBRI skill 2 (concession). Oral-argument convention: a judge’s yes/no question gets yes or no first.
Model it live: invite a student to ask you a hard question about the course design, and answer it in the three-part form.
Remind the room: under Criterion E the speaker takes at least one question personally and may be asked to explain one link in the claim-evidence map without notes.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 6: Discussing other teams

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
How the four minutes work
One team will be assigned to discuss another team’s presentation. So, every non-presenting team is the assigned discussant for one presenting team.








Minutes
Who
What




0:00–2:00
Assigned discussant team
Prepared response


2:00–4:00
Open floor
Any member of any team (time to show your participation)




Asking good questions counts toward participation, not toward the presenting team’s grade.

Sources Syllabus (“questioning the teams that present alongside you”; 2–4 minutes of questions); rubric callout on participation.
Assignments are posted on Teams before each session. If time is short, the assigned discussant uses two minutes and the open floor is cut to what remains; the assigned discussant is never cut.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The discussant is a pre-reviewer
The goals, from the conference discussant’s role:

Highlight the study’s relevance and contribution
Suggest constructive ways to make it stronger before the paper is due
Stimulate discussion with a question the room wants answered
Benefit both the presenters and the discussants: you learn to read an argument critically, which is your next three years of law school


Sources Ho, “How to discuss/review” deck, “Goals of a discussant.”
The reframing for this class: every team’s Round 5 package will be stronger if the other eleven teams took its Round 3 seriously. No paper is final.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The two-minute discussant template

Restate their claim in one sentence, at its strongest (steelman)
One strength, made specific: “The denominator point on slide 6 …”
One question aimed at a link: claim → mechanism, mechanism → evidence, or evidence → limitation
One suggestion that names a case, a source or a test


If you cannot do step 1, your question will miss. Restating their claim first also shows the presenters that you listened.

Sources Adapted from Ho, “How to discuss/review”; rubric Criterion E names the three links.
Divide the template within the discussant team: one member restates, one gives the strength, one asks, one suggests. That way a team of three to five shares the job evenly.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Good questions, weak questions


Questions that move the argument

“What would you expect to see if the rival were true?”
“What does the comparator do on this exact rule?”
“Your indicator is from 2016. Does the claim survive the newer data?”
“Which part of the package would elites capture first?”


Questions that do not

“Did you consider culture?” (too vague to answer)
“Isn’t that bad for democracy?” (a verdict, not a question)
“Can you go back to slide 3?” (unless you say why)
A two-minute speech that ends with “thoughts?”



Sources Rubric Rounds 2–5 requirements; dossier verification standard.
Each good question maps to a rubric requirement. Strong discussants read the rubric for the round before the session.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: What a discussant should not do
text:
What a discussant should not do
From the reviewer’s guide, adapted:

Do not criticize harshly or on surface matters: grammar, colors, a typo
Do not insert personal feelings: “I liked it, but …”
Do not give a verdict: “This reform would never pass”
Do not claim superiority: being a senior, a pre-law officer or a native speaker of the focal country’s language is not an argument


Be professional, scientific and constructive. The aim is to help, not to rank.

Sources Ho, “How to discuss/review,” the lists of practices to avoid and the positive guidance (“professional, scientific and constructive/positive”; “aim to help, not to categorize or classify”; “no paper is final”).
Connect to the syllabus statement on contested questions: engage arguments rather than people, and no student is required to represent a country or identity. A discussant who speaks from personal experience should still frame it as evidence, not authority.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Takeaways

One contestable sentence before any slide
Three supports, with the weak point conceded before anyone asks
Slides anchor; speech argues. About 43 words per slide, every number sourced
Divide by function, rotate the roles, rehearse twice against the clock
Answer first, then give the reason and the evidence
Discuss as a pre-reviewer: restate, one strength, one question, one suggestion
